Rough cost: about US$11,000–US$53,000 per market cluster (₹10,00,000–₹50,00,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, low to medium confidence)

India’s Street Vendors Act (2014) gives vendors 40% of the seats on each town vending committee and says no vendor may be evicted or relocated until a survey of existing vendors is complete: a hook for designing market cooling with vendors, not around them. (Street Vendors (Protection of Livelihood and Regulation of Street Vending) Act, 2014, on FAOLEX, https://faolex.fao.org/docs/pdf/ind194977.pdf)

### Bus stops and queues

Protects: Commuters, patients queuing at clinics, people waiting for rations or wages, and visitors.

Key caution: Put the shade where people actually stand, at the hours they wait.

- Cool waiting points: Shade, a bench, drinking water and a board showing the heat alert, at bus stops, clinics and ration shops. Keeps working with: Access for older and disabled people, and someone who refills the water. Avoid: Counting shelters built instead of people protected. Rough cost: about US$530–US$6,300 per site (₹50,000–₹6,00,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, medium confidence)

- Planted bus stops: Climbers on a frame that shade the stop more each year. Keeps working with: Watering and pruning. Avoid: Living shade with no water plan. Rough cost: No range solid enough to share: get local quotes.

- Trees where queues form: Canopy over the places people wait every day. Keeps working with: Root space, water and three years of care. Avoid: Planting where the queue isn’t. Rough cost: about US$21–US$84 per tree, with 2–3 years’ care (₹2,000–₹8,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, medium confidence)

- Shorter waits: Appointment slots, token systems and timed services so fewer people stand in the sun at midday. Keeps working with: Agreement from the clinic, office or transport operator. Avoid: Assuming shade is the only answer. Rough cost: No range solid enough to share: get local quotes.

Measuring how hot people actually feel on summer days in Tempe, Arizona, researchers found shade from buildings cooled most by day, then trees, then light structures such as sails. Air temperature barely differed between them, and every kind of shade held heat after sunset. (Middel et al., 50 Grades of Shade, Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society, https://par.nsf.gov/biblio/10230332-grades-shade)

### Heat and waterlogging

Protects: Neighbourhoods that bake in summer and flood in the monsoon, and the groundwater both depend on.

Key caution: Stop sewage and rubbish flowing in, and fund the desilting, before calling it blue-green.

- Sponge parks: Small parks shaped to hold, soak up and slowly release stormwater, with plants that cool the area around them. Keeps working with: An overflow, mosquito control and desilting before each monsoon. Avoid: Standing water. Rough cost: about US$8,400–US$18,000 per park (₹8,00,000–₹17,00,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, medium confidence); Chennai: 57 sponge parks commissioned for ₹7.67 crore, about ₹13.5 lakh each by our arithmetic

- Restored ponds and lakes: Desilted, protected water bodies with planted edges that store floodwater, recharge groundwater and cool their surroundings. Keeps working with: Sewage diverted away, and rubbish kept out. Avoid: Calling a polluted pond a cooling asset. Rough cost: about US$38,000–US$320,000 per pond (₹36,00,000–₹3,00,00,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, medium confidence); Chennai: one pond restored for ₹36 lakh

- Planted drains and rain gardens: Channels and hollows that slow, clean and soak up runoff from roofs and lanes. Keeps working with: Rubbish collection and an overflow. Avoid: Places where they will become open garbage drains. Rough cost: about US$5.3–US$32 per m² (₹500–₹3,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, low to medium confidence)

- Permeable paving: Paving that lets rain soak in instead of running off. Keeps working with: Regular cleaning so it does not clog. Avoid: Claiming it cools unless there is shade and moist soil too. Rough cost: about US$9.5–US$26 per m² (₹900–₹2,500 at Indian prices; planning estimate, low to medium confidence)

- Recharge pits: Small pits that send roof and courtyard runoff into the ground. Keeps working with: A filter, so polluted water does not reach shallow wells. Avoid: Recharging dirty runoff. Rough cost: about US$53–US$320 per pit (₹5,000–₹30,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, low to medium confidence)

Over four years, Greater Chennai Corporation restored 70 ponds for ₹144.34 crore and built 88 rainwater-harvesting parks for ₹14.74 crore. (The News Minute, https://www.thenewsminute.com/tamil-nadu/chennai-civic-body-ramps-up-pond-restoration-rainwater-harvesting-parks-ahead-of-monsoon)

Bangkok’s Benjakitti Forest Park, a former tobacco factory turned wetland, is designed to hold 87 million litres of water. (Mongabay, 2024, https://news.mongabay.com/2024/09/bangkok-turns-to-urban-forests-to-beat-worsening-floods/)

China’s sponge-city pilots in 30 cities (2014–2019) often built projects one at a time instead of as a city-wide system, struggled to get engineers and designers working together, and left cities worried about paying for more once pilot money ended. (McPhillips et al., chapter 7 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023, https://doi.org/10.4337/9781800376762)

Jakarta’s green space was about 5.2–5.6% of the city in 2024–25, sources differ, against a legal target of 30%, now pushed back to 2045. (Metro TV News, https://www.metrotvnews.com/read/KXyCWwmW-target-30-ruang-terbuka-hijau-jakarta-dikejar-hingga-2045)

### Greening where water is short

Protects: Trees, soil moisture and groundwater, and the long-term shade they give.

Key caution: Planting without water, soil care and a survival budget is not adaptation.

- Care for the trees you have: Better tree pits, mulch, compost and looser soil so existing trees take up water and survive. Keeps working with: A yearly care round. Avoid: Replanting instead of fixing why trees die. Rough cost: No range solid enough to share: get local quotes.

- Rainwater for trees: Store runoff from roofs and streets to water trees and gardens through dry spells. Keeps working with: Clean tanks and a plan for the dry months. Avoid: Planting with no water source at all. Rough cost: about US$210–US$2,100 per site (₹20,000–₹2,00,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, low to medium confidence)

- Treated wastewater for parks: Use treated water from a treatment plant for parks and tree corridors, so greenery does not compete with drinking water. Keeps working with: Treatment that is checked. Avoid: Untreated sewage on public land. Rough cost: No range solid enough to share: get local quotes.

- Street trees with three years’ care: Hardy, shade-giving species, chosen for the heat and drought ahead. Keeps working with: Species choice, root space, water and a named owner. Avoid: Counting planted trees. Rough cost: about US$21–US$84 per tree, with 2–3 years’ care (₹2,000–₹8,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, medium confidence)

- Dense mini-forests: Small, densely planted native woods on spare public land. Keeps working with: Water through the first years. Avoid: Assuming they beat ordinary shade trees on value. Rough cost: No range solid enough to share: get local quotes.

In Berlin’s Johannisthal park, more than 500 of 870 newly planted native trees died within ten years despite watering, so the shade and cooling never arrived. Across the city, about 44,000 street trees were cut between 2012 and 2019 and about 18,000 planted. (Hansen et al., chapter 10 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023, https://doi.org/10.4337/9781800376762)

In Santiago de Chile, how well a municipality manages its trees was the strongest predictor of whether they survive, and wealthier municipalities spend far more on it. (Hansen et al., chapter 10 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023, https://doi.org/10.4337/9781800376762)

### Making it last

Protects: Every asset above: who targets it, who opens it on an alert, who pays for upkeep, and who hears complaints.

Key caution: Often the most useful layer, and the easiest to leave unfunded.

- Link the heat plan to the assets: A ward or settlement plan that says which shelters, water points and cool spaces open at each alert level, and who opens them. Keeps working with: A yearly review with the people who use them. Avoid: A plan with no budget or named owners. Rough cost: about US$5,300–US$26,000 per plan (₹5,00,000–₹25,00,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, medium confidence)

- An upkeep agreement: A written deal between the council, community groups, schools or vendors on who repaints, waters, prunes, refills and repairs. Keeps working with: Money from the running budget, not only the building budget. Avoid: Paying to build without paying to maintain. Rough cost: about US$2,100–US$11,000 per year, for a cluster of assets (₹2,00,000–₹10,00,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, low to medium confidence)

- Map risk with the people exposed: Walk the area with workers, women, older and disabled people, migrants and renters to see who is exposed, why warnings fail, and where assets should go. Keeps working with: Repeating it as people and places change. Avoid: Relying on satellite heat maps alone. Rough cost: about US$5,300–US$21,000 per baseline (₹5,00,000–₹20,00,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, medium confidence)

- A way to complain and be heard: An accessible route for complaints and feedback, set up before work starts. Keeps working with: Someone who answers within a set time. Avoid: Starting work where affected people have no voice or remedy. Rough cost: about US$1,100–US$5,300 per set-up (₹1,00,000–₹5,00,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, medium confidence)

- Find the hooks in existing plans: Search city, disaster, water and climate plans and budgets for mandates and money that cooling can use. Keeps working with: Checking what you find with the officials concerned. Avoid: Assuming nothing exists because nobody uses the words “nature-based solutions”. Rough cost: about US$1,100–US$5,300 per review (₹1,00,000–₹5,00,000 at Indian prices; planning estimate, medium confidence)

In Melbourne, officials found money for new green infrastructure was usually available, but running budgets were under pressure and rarely increased, even as the area to maintain grew. (Hansen et al., chapter 10 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023, https://doi.org/10.4337/9781800376762)

In Santiago, without long-term financing, only better-off municipalities could take part in green-space programmes, because only they could afford the extra upkeep. (Hansen et al., chapter 10 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023, https://doi.org/10.4337/9781800376762)

Less than 10% of the climate finance that reaches cities goes to adaptation and resilience. (Cities Climate Finance Leadership Alliance, The State of Cities Climate Finance, 2021, https://www.climatepolicyinitiative.org/publication/the-state-of-cities-climate-finance/)

The IUCN Global Standard for Nature-based Solutions makes inclusive governance and equity one of its eight criteria. (IUCN Global Standard: the eight criteria, https://inbs.iucn.org/understand/8-criteria/)

### Questions before you choose

- Avoid: Cut the need for cooling first: shade, cooler roofs, air flow and trees.

- Improve: Where machines are needed, choose efficient ones that run on the power and water you really have.

- Expand access: Make sure the people most exposed can reach cooling and afford to keep it running.

(Clean Cooling Collaborative’s three goals, summarised by Philanthropy Asia Alliance, https://philanthropyasiaalliance.org/our-impact/climate---nature/calls-to-action/clean-cooling-collaborative)

- Does it need electricity, and is the supply reliable in the hottest weeks?

- What happens in a power cut: does it stop, or keep cooling without power?

- Does it need water, and where will that water come from in a dry spell?

- Who services or repairs it, and how fast?

- Who owns the running cost each year, and from which budget?

- Who can use it: renters, women, older people, people with disabilities?

Keep the outcomes apart. Name the outcome you want: a cooler room, people feeling comfortable, less heat strain on the body, fewer illnesses, or income kept. They are different. A cooler room does not prove better health, and comfort does not prove less strain, so measure the one you mean.

### Five traps that waste cooling money

- Buying before diagnosing: The asset is chosen before anyone has mapped who is exposed, where and why, so the shade ends up where nobody waits. Instead: Start with the people and places at risk, then choose.

- Built, with no one to keep it: It looks good for one season, then fades because no running budget or owner was set aside. Instead: Name who keeps each asset working after year one, and from which budget.

- Green without water: Trees, parks and green roofs go in with no water source, soil care or survival budget. Instead: Secure the water and three years of care before planting, and count trees that survive.

- Promising degrees you haven’t measured: A fixed temperature drop is promised from another place’s study. Instead: Log temperatures in treated and untreated places, and report what you measured.

- A list of activities, not a model: A proposal lists many activities, but none says who it protects, what it costs per unit, who owns it and what changes. Instead: For each option, name the users, the unit cost, the owner and the outcome.

### What changes the result

- Shade beats air temperature: In hot, sunny places, how hot people feel outdoors depends more on radiant heat from the sun and surfaces than on air temperature. Shade from buildings cooled most by day in a Tempe study, then trees, then light structures. (https://par.nsf.gov/biblio/10230332-grades-shade)

- Reflective paving can make walking hotter: In Los Angeles, coated roads were up to 6 °C cooler on the surface, but pedestrians above them received about 4 °C more radiant heat. Pair reflective surfaces with shade. (https://news.asu.edu/20200505-discoveries-street-smarts-required-heat-mitigation)

- Misting depends on humidity and air movement: In Singapore, a misting fan cut air temperature by about 1.5 °C and made people feel cooler. An overhead misting line without fans made no significant difference. (https://www.mdpi.com/2571-8797/3/1/11)

- Trees cool people more than thermometers show: WRI’s Cool Cities Lab puts the improvement trees make to thermal comfort at roughly 2–8 °C. That measures how hot people feel, which is not the same as air temperature. (https://www.wri.org/insights/urban-trees-cooling-potential)

### Putting a value on cooling

Modelled against housing built in its place, Guangzhou’s Haizhu wetland keeps the area within 600 m about 0.25 °C cooler on a typical summer day, and over 1 °C cooler on the site itself. Without it, productivity in nearby heavy outdoor work would fall by 2.5% in May and 16.1% in October, monthly risk of death would rise by 1.23–1.27% from June to September, and cooling bills would rise by about US$1.9 million over 30 years.

Most of the wetland’s US$146.8 million value comes from carbon and mental health, not cooling. So make the heat case in lives, heavy outdoor work and bills, not money alone. And the same cooling is worth most to people without air conditioning.

### Four heats in a home

A heat warning gives one number: the air temperature in the shade. A family under a tin roof lives with four heats at once, and the worst of it often comes after dark.

- Outdoor air: The temperature a weather station measures, in the shade. It is the number in almost every heat warning, but not what people feel inside a tin-roofed room.

- The roof: Sun-baked sheet metal gets far hotter than the air. Roofs of informal homes in Mumbai and Pune measured above 50 °C when the air was about 30 °C. (Urban Solutions: how informal settlements stay cool (informal measurements), https://urbansolutionsjournal.substack.com/p/how-are-informal-settlements-staying)

- Radiant heat: A hot ceiling gives off heat onto the people below, like standing near a stove, so a room can feel hotter than its air. This is what mean radiant temperature measures.

- Indoor air: The air inside, held in by thin walls, few windows and crowded rooms.

At night: After sunset the street starts to cool, but thin-roofed homes cool slowly. In low-income homes measured in Dhaka, Delhi, Faisalabad and rural Maharashtra, temperatures in tin-roofed houses swung 3–4 °C more over the month than the outdoor air, and stayed warmer indoors because they cooled so slowly at night. (Tasgaonkar et al., Scientific Data, 2022: indoor heat in low-income homes in South Asia, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-022-01314-5)

- 7.6 °C hotter, at most, for people in Ahmedabad’s informal settlements than for people in formal housing, in a survey of 860 households. (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/built-environment/articles/10.3389/fbuil.2022.874751/full)

- Up to 9 °C hotter indoors than outside, in pilot measurements in informal settlements in Kenya, Tanzania and Zimbabwe. (https://www.iied.org/sites/default/files/pdfs/2026-02/22697iied.pdf)

- 2–5 °C cooler indoors under reflective roof paint than under ordinary roofs, in Ahmedabad’s informal settlements. (https://www.nrdc.org/bio/anjali-jaiswal/cool-roofs-community-led-initiatives-four-indian-cities)

Indoors is not always hotter at midday: in an experiment in The Gambia, metal-roofed houses were about 1.4 °C cooler than the outdoor shade by day, but warmer at night. The danger is nights that do not cool.

For heat plans: Heat warnings measure the street. Heat plans should protect the room: count indoor and night-time heat, warn for hot nights, and pay for cooler roofs where people sleep.

## Worked heat action plans from Asia

How places in Asia have turned heat risk into a plan: what happened, what they decided, what changed, and who leads each action.

### Ahmedabad’s heat action plan (Ahmedabad, India, 2013 onwards)

What happened: In May 2010 a heatwave peaking at 46.8 °C caused an estimated 1,344 excess deaths in the city, 43% more than in the same weeks of 2009 and 2011.

What they decided: In 2013 the Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, with the Indian Institute of Public Health Gandhinagar and NRDC, launched South Asia’s first heat action plan: forecasts from the India Meteorological Department feed colour-coded alerts, departments act together, the public is warned, and health staff are trained. From 2017 the plan added cool roofs.

What changed: An evaluation estimated about 1,190 deaths a year were avoided after the plan began, compared with before it. The model has since spread to many other Indian cities and states.

- Heat action plans: led by City and local governments; paid by Not documented; Colour-coded alerts issued from IMD forecasts, with inter-agency response

- Heat-ready health services: led by Health authorities; paid by Not documented; Health staff trained to recognise and treat heat illness

- Cool, affordable housing: led by City and local governments; paid by Not documented; Cool roofs on homes in informal settlements and on public buildings

Source: Azhar et al., PLoS ONE, 2014: the 2010 heatwave https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0091831

Source: NRDC: the plan’s components and cool roofs https://www.nrdc.org/press-releases/ahmedabads-pioneering-plan-now-shielding-millions-killer-heat

Source: Hess et al., 2018: deaths avoided https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6236972/

### Thane’s ward-by-ward heat action plan (Thane, India, 2024 onwards)

What happened: In Thane, a fast-growing coastal city next to Mumbai, humidity and warm nights make heat more dangerous than the thermometer suggests, and the risk differs sharply from one ward to the next.

What they decided: In March 2024 the Thane Municipal Corporation and CEEW published a heat action plan built on a ward-level risk index of felt heat, warm nights and social vulnerability. A Heatwave Task Force across departments, chaired by an Additional Municipal Commissioner, runs it with emergency procedures. Measures include early warnings, cool roofs and pavements, water stations, shade, and heat preparedness in schools and hospitals.

What changed: Its effect on illness and deaths has not yet been publicly evaluated. What it shows is a plan that names who acts and where the risk is highest, before the season starts.

- Heat action plans: led by City and local governments; paid by Not documented; Ward-level risk index updated each season, with task-force actions logged against it

- Cooling centres and check-ins: led by City and local governments; paid by Not documented; Water stations and shaded areas in the highest-risk wards

- Cool, affordable housing: led by City and local governments; paid by Not documented; Cool roofs and cool pavements installed in high-risk wards

- Heat-ready health services: led by Health authorities; paid by Not documented; Hospitals and schools with heat preparedness procedures

Source: CEEW: How can Thane city tackle heatwave risks with a heat action plan https://www.ceew.in/publications/how-can-thane-city-tackle-heatwaves-risks-with-heat-action-plan

Source: Global Heat Health Information Network: Heat Action Plan for Thane City 2024 https://heathealth.info/resources/heat-action-plan-for-thane-city-2024/

### Tamil Nadu’s state-wide heat network (Tamil Nadu, India, 2024 onwards)

What happened: About 68% of Tamil Nadu’s people face 8–9 hours a day of strong heat stress from March to June, and 56% live where summer nights are warmer than the 1981–2011 average. The state’s 2019 heatwave action plan dealt mainly with short-term emergency response.

What they decided: In 2024 the State Planning Commission, with WRI India as knowledge partner and support from the British High Commission, convened a Heat Action Network of line departments, including disaster management, health, education, agriculture, environment and forests, and water. Together they wrote India’s first state-wide heat strategy, covering people, animals and ecosystems along three pathways: health and well-being, sustained resources and productivity, and cooling. It builds heat into schemes that already exist rather than starting new ones.

What changed: It is a strategy, not yet an evaluated programme. Departments are to take its recommendations to detailed project reports, with progress reviewed every 6–8 months. What it shows is a whole state, not one city, giving heat an owner across departments.

- Heat action plans: led by National governments; paid by Not documented; Departments in the Heat Action Network reporting progress every 6–8 months

- Heat-ready health services: led by Health authorities; paid by Not documented; Pregnancy-scheme check-ups that screen for heat risk (proposed)

- Cool, affordable housing: led by City and local governments; paid by Not documented; Slum redevelopment tenders that set a limit on heat gain through walls and roofs (proposed)

- Green, cool cities: led by National governments; paid by Public budget; Forest and tree cover rising from 23.8% towards 33% by 2030–31

Source: Tamil Nadu State Planning Commission, 2024: Beating the Heat https://spc.tn.gov.in/wp-content/uploads/Heat_Mitigation_Strategy.pdf

Source: WRI India: mapping the path to heat resilience in Tamil Nadu https://wri-india.org/perspectives/mapping-path-heat-resilience-tamil-nadu

Source: Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board, G.O. 215, 2023: the tree cover target https://tnpcb.gov.in/PDF/About_Us/Announcementgos/GoNo_215_101123.pdf

### Singapore’s heat rules for outdoor work (Singapore, 2023 onwards)

What happened: In one of the world’s densest, most humid cities, the commercial centre has measured up to about 7 °C warmer than the outskirts, and builders, shipyard and landscape workers labour outdoors through it. A study of 355 workers found each hot day cost a median S$21 in lost income.

What they decided: In 2023 the National Environment Agency launched a national heat stress advisory based on wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT), which counts humidity, sun and wind, with low, moderate and high levels. The Ministry of Manpower made employers check WBGT hourly at outdoor work, give at least 10 minutes’ shaded rest each hour for heavy work at 32 °C or above, help new workers acclimatise, and enforced it.

What changed: In March and June 2024 the ministry inspected 250 workplaces and acted against 78, mainly for missing shaded rest breaks and acclimatisation. The rules have since been revised and strengthened. Their effect on heat illness has not yet been publicly evaluated.

- Heat-safe work: led by National governments; paid by Employers; Outdoor worksites checking WBGT hourly and giving shaded rest breaks; workplaces inspected

- Heat action plans: led by Weather and climate services; paid by Not documented; Heat stress advisory with three WBGT risk levels, shown by location

- Green, cool cities: led by City and local governments; paid by Not documented; Districts modelled for cooling through Cooling Singapore

Source: Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment: Heat Stress Advisory, 2023 https://www.mse.gov.sg/latest-news/press-release-heat-stress-advisory/

Source: Ministry of Manpower: enhanced heat stress measures, 2023 https://www.mom.gov.sg/newsroom/press-releases/2023/1024-enhanced-measures-to-reduce-heat-stress-for-outdoor-workers

Source: HRD Asia: 78 of 250 worksites non-compliant, 2024 https://www.hcamag.com/asia/specialisation/employment-law/more-than-75-worksites-found-non-compliant-with-singapores-enhanced-heat-stress-measures-report/499570

Source: NUS Project HeatSafe, 2024 https://medicine.nus.edu.sg/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/PRESS-RELEASE_Project-HeatSafe-18MAR2024-FOR-IMMEDIATE-RELEASE.pdf

Source: Cooling Singapore https://www.thegpsc.org/sites/gpsc/files/cooling_singapore_-_digital_urban_climate_twin.pdf

### Dhaka acts before the heat peaks (Dhaka, Bangladesh, 2023 onwards)

What happened: Bangladesh’s ‘feels-like’ temperature has risen by about 4.5 °C since 1980, and parts of Dhaka run more than 10 °C hotter than the countryside. In April 2024 a long heatwave closed schools for about 33 million children.

What they decided: In 2023 Dhaka North City Corporation appointed Asia’s first Chief Heat Officer, a post paid for by the Arsht-Rock foundation rather than the city, to bring heat planning together. The same year the Bangladesh Red Crescent Society’s heatwave early action protocol was approved: when forecasts pass 38 °C, warnings, drinking water, cooling stations and cash grants go out before the peak.

What changed: On 21 April 2024 the protocol was activated for Dhaka, with about CHF 500,000 from the IFRC’s emergency fund to reach some 124,000 people. Its effect on illness and deaths has not been publicly evaluated. What it shows is money and a plan agreed before the heat, released by a forecast.

- Anticipatory action: led by Community and civil society groups; paid by Not documented; Days from a 38 °C forecast to cash, water and warnings reaching people

- Cooling centres and check-ins: led by Community and civil society groups; paid by Not documented; Cooling stations open at three locations during the heatwave

- Heat action plans: led by City and local governments; paid by Philanthropy; A Chief Heat Officer bringing the city’s heat planning together

Source: Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, 2024 https://www.climatecentre.org/13733/red-crescent-activates-early-action-protocol-for-heatwaves-in-dhaka/

Source: Arsht-Rock: Dhaka North’s Chief Heat Officer, 2023 https://onebillionresilient.org/2023/05/03/bushra-afreen-dhaka-chief-heat-officer/

Source: World Bank, 2025 https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2025/09/16/bangladesh-faces-health-and-economic-risks-from-rising-temperature-world-bank

Source: NBC News: school closures, 2024 https://www.nbcnews.com/news/world/schools-close-extreme-heat-philippines-bangladesh-asia-rcna149485

### Adapt the mechanism, not the city: how five cities organise for heat

From interviews with city officials in October and November 2024 and published material, as described in the report. These are examples of institutional practice, not evaluations of impact, and details may have changed since. Adapt the mechanism to your own powers, budgets and infrastructure; do not copy the city. (MCR2030, Urban Heat Risk Management Resource Package, 2025, https://mcr2030.undrr.org/publication/urban-heat-risk-management-resource-package)

#### Amadora, Portugal (pp. 15–20)

- The problem: Rising heat in a dense city with little room for green space, and older and low-income residents at most risk.

- How they work together: Civil Protection is the single focal point: it coordinates the departments, consolidates their information and runs the heatwave response, with the mayor’s support keeping heat a shared priority.

- Authority and money: About €1 million a year for heat activities within Civil Protection’s budget, which the city itself describes as not enough for comprehensive risk management.

- What reaches people: SMS alerts built with a private partner; the Red Cross, fire service and police help spread warnings; health and social teams visit 3,000–4,000 residents twice a week in summer; prepared cooled shelters.

- Still unresolved: Space for greenery in dense streets, and building codes still to be updated.

- Before adapting it, check: Is there one office that can convene the others and hold a heat budget? Who can do home visits at scale?

#### Incheon, Republic of Korea (pp. 21–27)

- The problem: More heatwave days and tropical nights, with elderly and low-income neighbourhoods most exposed; a sharp rise in heat illness in 2018.

- How they work together: National law treats heatwaves as a disaster, so heat sits inside the city’s disaster structure, led by a Natural Disaster Division, with district headquarters and field units.

- Authority and money: A local heat ordinance (2019) and national grants covering part of project costs; some protection is funded through welfare programmes rather than a heat budget.

- What reaches people: 1,340 heat shelters (2023), shelter locations shared in safety apps, nearly 7,000 volunteer ‘heatwave helpers’, and data analysis to find 52 priority areas for cooling facilities.

- Still unresolved: Competing land uses for urban forests, and long-term funding to scale up.

- Before adapting it, check: Does national law give local authorities a mandate and money for heat? Is there data on where older people live alone?

#### Cape Town, South Africa (pp. 34–40)

- The problem: Heat that falls hardest on low-income neighbourhoods and informal settlements, where most residents have little greenery and no air conditioning, pool or easy way to the beach.

- How they work together: A coordinating department convenes rather than implements, alongside existing structures: a business continuity committee, the disaster risk management centre and a climate forum.

- Authority and money: No dedicated national heat funding; the city relies on general grants, property taxes and tariffs.

- What reaches people: Outreach in the hottest areas, six spray parks in lower-income neighbourhoods, and cooling centres and real-time heat monitoring in planning.

- Still unresolved: Upkeep of green infrastructure, and resources to scale up public communication, including ‘message coupling’, which it plans to bring from its drought response to heat.

- Before adapting it, check: Is there a body that can convene without taking over others’ mandates? Who keeps essential services running in a heatwave?

#### Quito, Ecuador (pp. 28–33)

- The problem: A city centre up to 3 °C warmer than its surroundings, while a drought threatens water and hydropower.

- How they work together: Heat is managed inside the city’s long-term climate action plan, with an environment secretariat in the lead and the risk management secretariat alongside it.

- Authority and money: Funding from national, municipal, corporate and international sources; an ordinance on green and blue infrastructure.

- What reaches people: Nature-based solutions and planning rules, with community and international partners.

- Still unresolved: Heat is a lower national priority, and national weather data is incomplete.

- Before adapting it, check: Does your plan sit inside a wider climate plan with its own budget lines? Are the weather data you rely on maintained?

#### Nairobi, Kenya (pp. 41–45)

- The problem: Rapid development outpacing climate-sensitive planning, and the loss of green space.

- How they work together: Urban heat was made a priority for the first time; work sits with a small climate change department.

- Authority and money: Eight staff for all the department’s activities, no dedicated heat strategy yet, and limited funds.

- What reaches people: Forecasts from the national weather service reach the public through mainstream media; no dedicated heat warning yet.

- Still unresolved: Fragmented, siloed efforts across sectors; no local heat data; low public awareness.

- Before adapting it, check: Starting from little is common. What is the first decision, and the first piece of data, that would let the next step happen?

## Plain-language glossary of extreme heat

42 terms that come up again and again in extreme heat, explained in a sentence or two.

### What heat does to the body

- **Heatstroke**: A medical emergency. The body’s core temperature rises above about 40 °C and its cooling system fails. Without fast cooling it can kill or cause lasting organ damage.

- **Heat exhaustion**: The warning stage before heatstroke: heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness and nausea. Rest, water and cooling usually bring recovery.

- **Heat stress**: When the body takes in or makes more heat than it can shed, from hot air, humidity, sun and physical work.

- **Acclimatisation**: The body slowly adjusting to heat over one to two weeks. New and returning workers are most at risk until it has.

- **Excess deaths**: Deaths above the normal number for that place and time of year. Because death certificates rarely say “heat”, this is how the real toll of a heatwave is counted.

### How heat is measured

- **Wet-bulb temperature**: Heat and humidity combined into one number, read from a thermometer wrapped in a wet cloth. It shows whether sweat can still cool you. A wet-bulb temperature of 35 °C is often quoted as the limit of human survival; recent studies suggest the real limit is lower.

- **Dry heat and humid heat**: Dry heat is high temperature with low humidity: sweat still evaporates, but the body soaks up heat fast. It peaks in South Asia’s pre-monsoon months. Humid heat is warm, wet air in which sweat can’t evaporate, so the body can’t cool itself even at lower temperatures. It dominates Southeast Asia and builds through South Asia’s monsoon, and it is rising faster than dry heat. The two need different warnings and different cooling.

- **WBGT (wet-bulb globe temperature)**: The workplace measure of heat. It adds sun and wind to heat and humidity, and is used to set rest breaks and stop work.

- **Heat index**: The “feels-like” temperature in the shade, combining air temperature and humidity. In the Philippines, a heat index of 42 °C or more is officially a danger level.

- **Heatwave**: A spell of unusually hot weather for that place. There is no single global definition: each country sets its own thresholds.

- **Hot nights**: Nights that stay too hot for the body to recover from the day. They are often more dangerous than hot days, and they are rising faster.

- **Urban heat island**: Cities running several degrees hotter than the countryside around them, especially at night, because of concrete, traffic, waste heat and few trees.

- **Mean radiant temperature**: The heat your body takes in from the sun and from hot surfaces around it: roads, walls and roofs. In strong sun it shapes how hot you feel more than air temperature does, which is why shade matters so much.

- **Thermal comfort**: How hot or cold a person feels. It depends on air temperature, humidity, wind, sun, clothing and activity, not on air temperature alone.

### Acting before harm

- **Limits to adaptation**: The point beyond which adjusting no longer prevents harm. Places used to heat cope better with days of 30–35 °C, but a study of 2.7 million firms found no adaptation to days above 40 °C. Cutting emissions keeps more places below that limit.

- **Heat action plan**: A city’s or country’s plan for the heat season: who issues warnings, at what temperature, and what hospitals, employers and services do next.

- **Early warning system**: A forecast that reaches people in time, in a form they understand, with clear advice on what to do.

- **Anticipatory action**: Acting on a forecast, before a disaster peaks, by releasing pre-agreed money and help when a trigger is reached.

- **Cooling centre**: A public place, such as a library, school or community hall, kept cool during heatwaves for people with no cool space at home.

### Money and protection

- **Parametric insurance**: Insurance that pays out automatically when a measured trigger, such as a temperature threshold, is crossed. There is no claim form and no damage assessment.

- **Basis risk**: When the trigger and the real loss don’t match: people suffer from the heat, but the threshold isn’t crossed and no payout comes.

- **Risk pool**: A group of countries, cities or insurers that share the cost of disasters, so no single member carries a catastrophe alone.

- **Social protection**: Public support such as pensions, cash transfers and unemployment benefits that keeps households out of poverty when income stops.

### Cooling, land and systems

- **Passive cooling**: Cooling a building without using power: shade, airflow, insulation, orientation and reflective surfaces.

- **Cool roof**: A roof painted or built to reflect sunlight, so less heat reaches the room below.

- **Refrigerant**: The fluid inside air conditioners and fridges that carries heat away. Many common ones are powerful greenhouse gases if they leak.

- **Black carbon**: Soot from diesel, wood, coal and brick kilns. It warms the air, and when it settles on snow and ice it darkens them so they melt faster.

- **Vicious cycle**: A harm that feeds itself: each turn of the loop makes the next one worse. This map shows where those loops could be interrupted.

- **Maladaptation**: A response to heat that makes things worse elsewhere or later, such as air conditioners that cool a room but heat the street.

- **Albedo**: How much sunlight a surface reflects. A white roof has a high albedo and stays cooler; dark asphalt has a low albedo and stores heat.

### Nature in the city

- **Evapotranspiration**: Water evaporating from soil and leaves. It draws heat out of the air, so well-watered plants cool their surroundings. Plants short of water stop cooling.

- **Nature-based solutions**: Using living systems such as trees, wetlands, soils and water to tackle problems like heat and flooding while also benefiting people and nature. A park only works as one if it is planned for those benefits and kept alive.

- **Ecosystem services**: The benefits people get from nature: shade and cooling, cleaner air and water, rain soaking into the ground, food and places to rest. The same service is worth most to those with the fewest alternatives, such as cooling for people without air conditioning.

- **Blue-green infrastructure**: A network of water (blue) and plants and soil (green), such as rivers, ponds, wetlands, parks and planted drains, designed to manage rain and heat together.

- **Grey infrastructure**: Engineered, mostly concrete systems such as pipes, drains, embankments and pumps. Many good solutions mix grey and green.

- **Sponge city**: A city designed to soak up, store, clean and slowly release rainwater through parks, wetlands, permeable ground and planted drains, not only pipes. China piloted it in 30 cities from 2014 to 2019; Chennai and Bangkok are building sponge parks.

- **Co-benefits**: The extra gains a measure brings beyond its main aim, such as a park built to hold floodwater that also cools the street and gives children somewhere to play.

- **Ecosystem-based adaptation**: Using nature to help people adapt to climate change, such as mangroves against storm surges or trees for shade. A kind of nature-based solution.

- **Green gentrification**: When a new park or greening raises rents and land prices so much that the poorer residents it was meant to help are pushed out.

- **Environmental justice**: A fair share of environmental benefits and harms, and a fair say in decisions about them. Poorer neighbourhoods are often hotter and less green.

### Also explained on the map

- **Aquifer**: Underground layers of rock or sand that hold groundwater, the water that wells and pumps draw from.

- **Agroforestry**: Growing trees alongside crops or livestock. The trees shade the soil, help it hold moisture and give farmers another source of income.

## Organisations working on extreme heat

204 organisations across Asia and the world already working on parts of the web of extreme heat. Inclusion describes relevant published work. It does not imply partnership, affiliation or endorsement.

### Global networks and organisations

- Global Heat Health Information Network (WHO, WMO and NOAA): A member-driven forum of scientists, practitioners and policymakers. Its resource library gathers guidance on heat warnings, heat action plans and case studies, heat at work and heat in cities. (https://heathealth.info/resource-library/)

- International Labour Organization: Sets out the evidence and standards for protecting workers from heat stress. (https://www.ilo.org/resource/news/increase-heat-stress-predicted-bring-productivity-loss-equivalent-80)

- UNICEF: Tracks how heatwaves and other climate hazards disrupt children’s schooling. (https://www.unicef.org/reports/learning-interrupted-global-snapshot-2024)

- Zurich Climate Resilience Alliance: An alliance of humanitarian, development and research partners with Zurich Insurance Group. In 2024 it expanded from floods to extreme heat, with work in countries including Bangladesh and Nepal. Its 2026 study of heat early warning systems covered eight countries, among them Bangladesh, Nepal, Pakistan, the Philippines and Vietnam. (https://zcralliance.org/resources/?q=heat)

- Heat Resilience Action (HERA), formerly Climate Resilience for All: Works on extreme heat with a focus on women and low-income communities. With SEWA and Swiss Re, it combined insurance payouts and cash for lost income after India’s 2024 heatwaves. (https://heranow.org/resources/as-extreme-heat-threats-grow-can-heat-insurance-offer-protection/)

- UNEP Cool Coalition: A global network for clean, efficient cooling and cooler cities. With the COP30 Presidency, it runs Beat the Heat, an initiative supporting cities in the Global South with heat assessments and cooling action. (https://coolcoalition.org)

- Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre: Wrote the Heatwave Guide for Cities with more than 25 partners, covering how cities prepare for, respond to and learn from heatwaves. (https://preparecenter.org/resource/heatwave-guide-for-cities)

- Sustainable Energy for All: Measures who lacks access to cooling through its Chilling Prospects series. (https://www.seforall.org/our-work/research-analysis/chilling-prospects-series/chilling-prospects-global-access-to-cooling-gaps-2023)

- International Energy Agency: Analyses cooling demand and how efficiency standards can cut it. (https://www.iea.org/reports/the-future-of-cooling)

- Practical Action: Connects heat risk intelligence, local action, practical technology, institutions and finance, following a Sense → Decide → Act → Sustain logic. In Nepal, Dhangadhi’s heat action plan links temperature, humidity and health data, hotspot mapping and community views to thresholds and set municipal responses. In Bangladesh, heat is being built into early warning and livelihood work. A partner in the Zurich Climate Resilience Alliance. (https://practicalaction.org/news-stories/zurich-climate-resilience-alliance-to-expand-focus-on-destructive-extreme-heat/)

- People’s Courage International: Works on safe migration and labour protection for migrant workers in South and Southeast Asia. Its Migrants Resilience Collaborative supports more than seven million households. (https://www.weforum.org/organizations/peoples-courage-international/)

- World Bank: Its 2026 report A Livable Future finds extreme heat already costs South Asia the equivalent of about 31 million full-time jobs a year, and sets out how cities can protect jobs and growth. (https://www.worldbank.org/en/region/sar/publication/a-livable-future-protecting-jobs-and-growth-from-extreme-heat-in-south-asia-s-cities)

- World Meteorological Organization: With WHO, runs the South Asia Climate–Health Desk with India’s meteorological agencies, turning weather and climate information into health protection. (https://wmo.int/node/38332)

- C40 Cities: Its Cool Cities Accelerator brings together cities including Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Mumbai and Singapore on early warnings, building standards and tree cover. (https://www.deccanherald.com/india/karnataka/bengaluru/bengaluru-joins-global-coalition-to-beat-extreme-heat-3786724)

- Vital Strategies: Through the Partnership for Healthy Cities, supports Bangkok to pilot heat-health action in high-risk districts: outdoor worker protection, cooling spaces and drinking water. (https://www.nationthailand.com/pr-news/40071201)

- Global Buildings Performance Network: Works on residential building codes in India and Southeast Asia, where demand for cooling homes is rising fastest. (https://gbpn.org/news-gbpn-sharpens-its-focus-decarbonising-housing-india-and-south-east-asia)

- Start Network: Its members run heatwave anticipatory action in Pakistan, releasing funds automatically when forecasts cross agreed triggers. (https://startnetwork.org/news-and-blogs/getting-ahead-deadly-heat)

- Mercy Corps: A Zurich Climate Resilience Alliance partner leading work on extreme heat in Nepal, where the southern plains passed 40 °C on 50 days in 2024. (https://europe.mercycorps.org/sites/default/files/2025-09/too-hot-to-ignore.pdf)

- United Nations Development Programme (UNDP): Helps governments connect heat resilience with health systems, urban planning and finance. Its work includes a financing strategy for tackling urban heat in Bangkok. (https://www.undp.org/thailand/publications/bangkok-financing-strategy-tackling-urban-heat)

- UN-Habitat: Develops guidance on urban heat management, helping cities combine planning, building design, green infrastructure and cooling to protect vulnerable residents. (https://unhabitat.org/handbook-on-urban-heat-management-in-the-global-south)

- UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR): Helps governments strengthen heat risk governance through practical assessment tools, coordinated planning and investment across sectors and levels of government. (https://www.undrr.org/our-work/extreme-heat-resilience)

- Resilient Cities Network: Works with cities and communities on heat resilience, including indoor heat monitoring and locally designed cooling in Southeast Asian cities. (https://resilientcitiesnetwork.org/heat-stays-in-peoples-homes/)

- ICLEI South Asia: Supports cities with heat risk assessments, heat action plans, urban greening and preparedness tools in India, Nepal and Bangladesh. (https://southasia.iclei.org/news/extreme-heat-new-knowledge-products-highlight-need-to-build-resilience-adaptation/)

- United Cities and Local Governments Asia-Pacific (UCLG ASPAC): Provides technical assistance for urban heat resilience, including work with Iloilo City in the Philippines and Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh. (https://uclg-aspac.org/turning-the-heat-into-action-how-iloilo-city-and-coxs-bazar-respond-to-urban-heat/)

- Women in Informal Employment: Globalizing and Organizing (WIEGO): Documents how heat affects informal workers’ health and earnings, and develops worker education, policy recommendations and protection guidance with local organisations. (https://www.wiego.org/research-library-publications/working-heat-street-vendors-delhi-india/)

- International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC): Mobilises national societies and communities to prepare for heatwaves and reach people at risk, including through its global Heat Action Day campaign. (https://www.ifrc.org/get-involved/campaign-us/heat-action-day)

- Climate and Development Knowledge Network (CDKN): Supports locally relevant climate knowledge and partnerships, including heat early warning, urban health resilience and preparedness planning in India. (https://cdkn.org/project/urban-health-and-climate-resilience-in-india)

- United for Efficiency (UNEP-led): Helps countries strengthen appliance efficiency policies and standards, including work across Southeast Asia on efficient, climate-friendly air conditioning. (https://united4efficiency.org/project/asean/)

- Humanity & Inclusion (HI): Sets out disability-inclusive approaches to climate action, including accessible early warnings, which people with disabilities often lack. A heat-specific programme in Asia is not confirmed. (https://www.hi-canada.org/sn_uploads/Disability-Inclusive-approaches-to-climate-action_1.pdf)

- Human Rights Watch: Documents how extreme heat endangers older people and people with disabilities, and how heat and climate plans leave them out. (https://www.hrw.org/news/2023/06/30/extreme-heat-signals-need-inclusive-climate-action)

### Governments and regional bodies in Asia

- National Disaster Management Authority, India: Issues national guidance for state and city heat action plans. (https://ndma.gov.in)

- National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, Nepal: Issued Nepal’s first federal heat plan in 2024. (https://english.onlinekhabar.com/reassessing-nepals-heat-wave-response-lessons-from-2024-and-the-way-forward.html)

- Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, with IIPH Gandhinagar and NRDC: Launched South Asia’s first heat action plan in 2013: early warnings, public outreach and training for medical staff. (https://www.nrdc.org/press-releases/new-evidence-shows-pioneering-heat-action-plan-helps-millions-avoid-killer-heat)

- Dhaka North City Corporation: Appointed Asia’s first Chief Heat Officer in 2023, focused on cooling the poorest neighbourhoods. (https://www.dhakatribune.com/bangladesh/310693/arsht-rock-bangladesh%E2%80%99s-first-chief-heat-officer)

- Nepal Red Cross Society: Published the Dhangadhi Heat Action Plan in 2025 with the Climate Centre, setting out when and where to act before and during heatwave days in a city that passes 40 °C every year. (https://www.climatecentre.org/publications/16234/dhangadhi-heat-action-plan-2025/)

- Department of Education, Philippines: Lets school heads suspend in-person classes when the heat index is dangerous, and moved the school year back to a June start to keep classes out of the hottest months. (https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/1940232/deped-all-set-for-june-school-opening-in-25)

- Bangladesh Red Crescent Society: Runs an early action protocol for heat, first activated in April 2024 during Dhaka’s longest recorded heatwave. (https://www.atachcommunity.com/our-impact/case-studies/bangladesh-early-action-protocol-for-heat-events/)

- ICIMOD: Monitors the Himalaya’s snow and ice, and helps brick kilns switch to cleaner technology that cuts the soot darkening the glaciers. (https://www.downtoearth.org.in/climate-change/existing-solutions-could-slash-soot-emissions-by-80-by-2030-icimod)

- Asian Development Bank: Supports heat resilience in Asian cities, including technical assistance on heat stress among women and girls in Bangladesh, Cambodia, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Tajikistan. Its 2026 report on the heat crisis in Thailand and Southeast Asia calls for mobilising public and private finance, and proposes a heat action plan for Thailand. (https://www.preventionweb.net/publication/beating-heat-investing-pro-poor-solutions-urban-resilience)

- UN ESCAP: Helps fast-growing cities in South and Southeast Asia plan for extreme urban heat, working with Iloilo City and Cox’s Bazar. (https://unescap.org/our-work/environment-development/cities-for-a-sustainable-future/addressing-urban-extreme-heat)

- India Meteorological Department and IITM Pune: Issue India’s heatwave forecasts and work with WHO and WMO on the South Asia Climate–Health Desk. (https://wmo.int/node/38332)

- PAGASA, Philippines: Issues heat index warnings with danger levels that local governments use to decide when to suspend classes. (https://www.gmanetwork.com/regionaltv/news/115185/pagasa-urges-public-to-brace-for-more-intense-heat/story/)

- Ministry of Manpower, Singapore: Requires hourly wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT) checks on outdoor worksites, shaded rest breaks when heat stress is high, and time for new workers to acclimatise, and enforces the rules. (https://www.mom.gov.sg/newsroom/press-releases/2023/1024-enhanced-measures-to-reduce-heat-stress-for-outdoor-workers)

- National Centre for Disease Control, India: Leads heat-health guidance, training and surveillance through India’s National Programme on Climate Change and Human Health. (https://ncdc.mohfw.gov.in/includes/About/CentresAndDivision/CEOH.php)

- National Environment Agency, Singapore: Issues public heat stress advisories through myENV and weather services, so people can adjust outdoor activity as heat rises. (https://www.nea.gov.sg/media/news/news/index/new-heat-stress-advisory-launched-to-guide-public-on-minimising-risk-of-heat-related-illnesses)

- Hong Kong Observatory: Issues very hot weather warnings with protective advice, including for people more vulnerable to heat. (https://www.hko.gov.hk/en/wservice/warning/coldhot.htm)

- Thai Meteorological Department: Publishes heat index forecasts and works with health authorities to help people respond to dangerous heat and humidity. (https://hpc.tmd.go.th/NCEP2/)

- Provincial Disaster Management Authority, Sindh (Pakistan): Coordinated the 2024 heatwave response across rural Sindh: by late June, 40 humanitarian partners ran 294 heat stabilisation camps, with awareness sessions and transport to heatstroke centres. (https://reliefweb.int/report/pakistan/pdma-sindh-situation-report-heatwave-2024-28-june-2024)

### Research and evidence

- Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW): Assessed heat risk in all 734 districts of India in 2025, finding 57% of districts, home to three in four Indians, at high or very high risk. Its 2026 heat-health reports for the GHHIN South Asia hub cover India, Nepal, Bangladesh and Bhutan, and it helped Thane build its heat action plan. (https://www.ceew.in/publications?field_focus_area_tid=All&field_pub_type_tid=All&field_authors_target_id_selective=All&title=heat)

- Lancet Countdown: Tracks heat deaths, lost working hours and other health impacts of climate change every year. (https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(24)01822-1)

- NUS Heat Resilience & Performance Centre: Hosts the Southeast Asia Hub of the Global Heat Health Information Network, bringing governments and partners together on heat and health. (https://medicine.nus.edu.sg/newsletters/issue54/dossier/nus-centre-designated-southeast-asia-hub-for-global-heat-health-info-exchange)

- Cornell Global Labor Institute: With Schroders, mapped heat and flood risk in garment hubs including Dhaka, Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City and Phnom Penh, and found few fashion brands require heat protection in their supplier codes. (https://www.ilr.cornell.edu/global-labor-institute/higher-ground-fashions-climate-breakdown)

- International Rice Research Institute (IRRI): Showed from its Philippine farm that warmer nights cut rice yields, and breeds rice that copes better with heat. (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0403720101)

- icddr,b: Works with Bangladesh’s Department of Agricultural Extension and others on HeatShield, which helps farmers cope with extreme heat. (https://www.rockefellerfoundation.org/perspective/who-owns-the-response-to-heat-in-bangladesh-everyone-does/)

- BRAC James P Grant School of Public Health: Part of a South Asian partnership with CEEW, NRDC, UN ESCAP and the Global Heat Health Information Network assessing heat-health action across countries. (https://www.ceew.in/sites/default/files/ceew-sfc-nrdc-unescap-brac-jpgsph-ghhin-countries-synthesis-press-release.pdf)

- IISER Pune: Leads the South Asia Scientific Research Consortium on how heat affects different populations, with Rockefeller Foundation support. (https://wmo.int/node/38332)

- International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED): Has researched the health and economic toll of heat stress on informal workers in urban Bangladesh. (https://www.iied.org/node/83215)

- Heat and Health Research Centre, University of Sydney: Tested low-cost cooling for Bangladeshi garment workers: fans, drinking water and reflective roofs recovered much of the 12–15% output lost to heat. (https://www.sydney.edu.au/news-opinion/news/2025/10/21/garment-factories-are-sweltering--these-simple-fixes-could-keep-.html)

- Salata Institute, Harvard University: Published Critical Perspectives on Extreme Heat in India in 2026, covering heat action plans, insurance and informal work. (https://salatainstitute.harvard.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/April-2026-Critical-Perspectives-on-Extreme-Heat-in-India_web.pdf)

- WRI India: Works on heat mitigation planning with Indian cities, including greening and cooling pilots in Kochi and Mumbai and the Bengaluru Heat Collective. (https://india.mongabay.com/2025/04/safeguarding-indian-cities-from-heat-in-conversation-with-sudeshna-chatterjee-interview/)

- Good Business Lab: Researching heat, health and gender in India’s and Bangladesh’s garment sector, 2025–2027. (https://lirneasia.net/futureworksasia/projects/heat-health-and-gender/)

- Integrated Research and Action for Development (IRADe): Develops heat hotspot assessments and gender-sensitive heat action plans in India, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka. (https://irade.org/website/ongoing-projects-2/)

- Indian Institute for Human Settlements (IIHS): Researches urban heat and tests passive and low-energy cooling shelters that give outdoor workers safe places to rest and recover. (https://iihs.co.in/publication/evaluating-indoor-thermal-resilience-of-passive-and-low-power-cooling-shelters-for-outdoor-workers-in-india/)

- Center for Study of Science, Technology and Policy (CSTEP): Builds heat intelligence and decision-support tools for Indian cities, including the BHRIGU National Heat Insights Explorer. (https://cstep.in/projects/building-heat-resilience-in-indias-growing-urbanscapes-bhrigu/)

- The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI): Researches thermal comfort, efficient buildings and sustainable cooling, combining passive design with better cooling equipment. (https://www.teriin.org/project/sheetal-alliance-sustainable-habitat-energy-efficiency-and-thermal-comfort-all-cooling)

- Sustainable Futures Collaborative: Studies heat action plans and their implementation gaps, and how policy, finance and social protection can make heat resilience last. (https://www.sustainablefutures.org/blog/beyond-heat-action-plans-inclusive-heat-policy-needs-grounded-research-and-collaborative-action/)

- Karachi Urban Lab: Researches how low-income residents and informal workers in Karachi live with heat, including access to shade, cooling, water and reliable infrastructure. (https://www.karachiurbanlab.com/projects/cool-infrastructures-life-with-heat-in-the-off-grid-city.html)

- Singapore Management University, Urban Institute: Studies urban heat vulnerability and cooling through the Cooling Singapore collaboration, linking neighbourhood conditions to climate-sensitive planning. (https://cityperspectives.smu.edu.sg/wcs-2026/pages/research/cooling-singapore-solutions-for-a-heat-resilient-city.html)

- Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST): Researches urban heat, ventilation, tree canopy and building cooling in dense cities. (https://researchportal.hkust.edu.hk/en/publications/evaluating-energy-and-microclimate-impacts-of-passive-and-high-ef/)

- London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine: Researches heat-related health risks and adaptation, including ways to protect pregnant women and newborns, with partners in Africa and Pakistan. (https://www.lshtm.ac.uk/newsevents/news/2024/tackling-premature-births-face-climate-change)

- Sri Ramachandra Institute of Higher Education and Research: Studies occupational heat exposure among workers in India, including physiological strain, dehydration, kidney health and productivity. (https://iqac.sriramachandra.edu.in/iqacreq/sdg13/environmental-education-measures-1332evd2.pdf)

- CEPT University, Centre for Advanced Research in Building Science and Energy: Tests building and cooling performance, including work with RMI on air conditioners that cool efficiently in real heat and humidity. (https://rmi.org/resources/bringing-super-efficient-air-conditioners-to-the-market/)

- Heat Island Group, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory: Researches reflective roofs and pavements, urban trees and other measures that cool buildings and cities while cutting energy use. (https://heatisland.lbl.gov/index.php/cool-science)

- Heat Policy Innovation Hub, Duke University: Brings researchers, governments and communities together on heat policy, including adaptable heat action planning tools. (https://climate.duke.edu/annual-report/items/heat-policy-innovation-hub/)

- CIMMYT (International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center): Breeds heat-tolerant maize for rainfed smallholder farms with national research institutes and seed companies. Hybrids are now grown in Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal and Pakistan. (https://www.cimmyt.org/projects/heat-stress-tolerant-maize-for-asia/)

- ICRISAT: Improves the heat and drought tolerance of dryland crops such as pearl millet, sorghum and chickpea, which feed rainfed farming households across South Asia. (https://www.icrisat.org/key-impacts/climate-action)

- Nature Conservation Foundation: Has monitored Lakshadweep’s reefs since 1998 and links their decline to repeated marine heatwaves, with consequences for island fishing communities. (https://www.ceab.csic.es/en/?p=17541)

### Working on the ground

- Self Employed Women’s Association (SEWA): Protects women informal workers’ income in heatwaves. After the May 2024 heatwaves, more than 46,000 members received insurance payouts. (https://www.swissre.com/our-business/public-sector-solutions/insights/parametric-structure-for-sewa-in-south-east-asia.html)

- Mahila Housing Trust: Cools homes in informal settlements with reflective and modular roofs, and runs heat income insurance for women workers. (https://citizenmatters.in/new-cool-roof-solutions-heat-in-informal-settlements/)

- ADRA India: Ran an anticipatory heatwave response in 2025 with national and district authorities. (https://adraindia.org/anticipatory-heatwave-response-in-2025/)

- HomeNet Thailand: With WIEGO, surveyed more than 1,000 informal workers in Bangkok on heat: nearly 80% had cut their hours. A trusted link between workers and authorities. (https://www.wiego.org/research-library-publications/climate-change-and-heat-stress-impacts-bangkok-thailand/)

- All India Disaster Mitigation Institute (AIDMI): An Ahmedabad-based institute that helps Indian states, districts and cities turn heat warnings into local action. It supports local heat action planning, surveyed 121 street vendors, auto drivers and construction and domestic workers in Lucknow on how heat hits their work, offers Afat Vimo disaster microinsurance to low-income families, and runs a regular southasiadisasters.net series on extreme heat. (https://aidmi.org/key-resources-on-extreme-heat-cooling/)

- SEEDS: Combines building-level heat risk mapping, community preparedness and affordable cool roofs for vulnerable urban settlements in India. (https://www.seedsindia.org/portfolio/partnering-to-strengthen-climate-resilience/)

- SELCO Foundation: Develops sustainable energy and cooling for underserved communities, including thermally comfortable buildings, cool roofs and decentralised cold storage. (https://selcofoundation.org/built-environments/)

- HeatWatch India: Focuses on heat and worker protection through research, heat exposure mapping, practical education and a public directory of cooling centres. (https://cooling-centres.heatwatch.in/about)

- Chintan Environmental Research and Action Group: Works with waste picker communities on heat awareness, hotspot mapping and practical ways to cut heat exposure at home and at work. (https://www.chintan-india.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/HEAT-SOLUTIONS-FOR-WEB-final.pdf)

- Hasiru Dala: Works with waste workers in Bengaluru to document heat-related health and income losses and press for water, shade, safer housing and workplace protection. (https://hasirudala.in/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/HW-HD-report_final.pdf)

- Janpahal: Works with informal worker organisations and WIEGO on heat protection, worker education and policy dialogue for street vendors. (https://www.wiego.org/advocacy-worker-education-resources/working-under-heat-delhi/)

- Jan Sahas: Works with migrant and informal workers on community-led heat resilience, and funds premiums for a temperature-triggered heat cover with Go Digit and K.M. Dastur. (https://indiaclimatecollaborative.org/blog/centering-workers-in-heat-resilience-from-lived-experience-to-systemic-action)

- Save the Children International: Addresses heat risks to children through awareness, drinking water and advocacy on education and health, including heat-related school closures in Bangladesh. (https://www.savethechildren.net/news/heat-stricken-bangladesh-extends-school-closures)

- Watershed Organisation Trust (WOTR): Sends heat-health advisories by SMS to farmers, farm labourers and rural job-scheme workers in drought-prone Marathwada, built with the India Meteorological Department, alongside its watershed work. (https://cdkn.org/story/heat-health-advisories-rural-india-learning-during-pandemic-era)

- BRAC: In Bangladesh’s April 2024 heat emergency, mobilised 50,000 community health workers to raise awareness, with a focus on families with pregnant women, and is piloting heat-reduction ideas in urban slums. (https://bracusa.org/bangladesh_heat_emergency/)

- HelpAge International: Works with older people’s associations in Bangladesh and Pakistan on disaster risk, including heatwaves and early warning, and speaks up for older farm labourers and street vendors exposed to heat. (https://helpage.org/tags/bangladesh)

- Centre for Disability in Development (CDD), with CBM: Runs disability-inclusive disaster risk and climate adaptation in Bangladesh, including coastal sub-districts, where heatwaves are among the hazards. A heat-specific programme is not confirmed. (https://cbm.org/news/news-initiatives/news-hua/persons-with-disabilities-in-the-context-of-climate-change-adaptation-in-bangladesh)

### Cooling solutions

- CLASP: Helps governments and manufacturers make cooling appliances more efficient and affordable, including efficient fans in India. (https://www.clasp.ngo/about/insights/making-efficient-affordable-fans-the-standard-in-india/)

- RMI: Advances efficient air conditioning, passive cooling and reflective roofs through research, field demonstrations and innovation support. (https://rmi.org/resources/reshaping-the-future-of-heating-and-cooling/)

- Cool Roof Rating Council: Provides technical guidance on reflective roofs, walls and pavements that reduce building heat. (https://coolroofs.org/news/new-cool-surfaces-toolkit-site-provides-public-with-resources-and-knowledge-base)

- Ecozen: Makes solar-powered cold rooms that help farmers keep produce from spoiling where power is unreliable. (https://www.ecozensolutions.com/ecofrost)

- Tarutium Global Consulting (formerly TARU Leading Edge): Provides climate risk and resilience planning, including urban heat assessment and heatwave management guidance. (https://tarutium.com/hydro-meteorological-resilient-action-plans/)

### Insurance and finance

- Atlantic Council Climate Resilience Center (formerly Arsht-Rock): Places Chief Heat Officers in cities, and with SEWA tested the world’s first parametric insurance for extreme heat in 2023. (https://onebillionresilient.org/project/extreme-heat-protection-initiative/)

- Swiss Re: Designed heat insurance for SEWA members with payout triggers set for each of 23 locations’ own climate. (https://www.swissre.com/our-business/public-sector-solutions/insights/parametric-structure-for-sewa-in-south-east-asia.html)

- IBISA: Launched a parametric heat-index product in Ahmedabad in 2024 that pays women workers when heat cuts their working hours, and Ushma Kavach, which protects dairy farmers against heat-stress losses. (https://www.icmif.org/news_story/ibisa-launches-a-new-parametric-heat-index-product-in-india-to-protect-women-workers-from-heat-induced-wage-losses/)

- ICICI Lombard: Carries the risk on heat insurance for women workers in India, including IBISA’s heat-index product. (https://www.icmif.org/news_story/ibisa-launches-a-new-parametric-heat-index-product-in-india-to-protect-women-workers-from-heat-induced-wage-losses/)

- Howden: Insurance broker working on parametric heat insurance and catastrophe bonds that give local governments and relief organisations money to act during heatwaves. (https://www.howdengroup.com/uk-en/news-insights/article-name/parametric-insurance-for-extreme-heat-protecting-people-in-a-warming-world)

- Climate Policy Initiative: Analyses how heat resilience in India is financed, and where money is missing. (https://www.climatepolicyinitiative.org/financing-indias-heat-resilience/)

- International Finance Corporation (IFC): Supports private investment in sustainable cooling, including district cooling, cooling-as-a-service and temperature-controlled food supply chains. (https://www.ifc.org/en/what-we-do/programs-projects/sustainable-cooling)

- Basel Agency for Sustainable Energy (BASE): Develops financing models for sustainable cooling, such as cooling-as-a-service, where customers pay for cooling and providers own and maintain the equipment. (https://energy-base.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/10.CaaS_Instrument-Analysis-Paper_FINAL_09.17.19.pdf)

- Blue Marble: Designs insurance for underserved communities, including the extreme heat income insurance pilot developed with SEWA and Arsht-Rock in India. (https://www.transre.com/what-we-do/blue-marble-microinsurance/)

- CelsiusPro Group, including Global Parametrics: Develops parametric protection; Global Parametrics manages Natural Disaster Fund risk capacity used for heat insurance for women informal workers in India. (https://www.celsiuspro.com/news-1/livestream-replay-uninsurable-how-the-natural-disaster-fund-contributes-to-close-the-protection-gap)

- K.M. Dastur Insurance and Reinsurance Brokers: Indian broker and partner, with Go Digit and Jan Sahas, in a temperature-triggered heat cover that pays migrant workers automatically. (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/godigit_digitinsurance-heatinsurance-parametricinsurance-activity-7341758644490764288-StEd)

- Go Digit General Insurance: Indian insurer offering temperature-triggered heat cover for workers, with Jan Sahas and K.M. Dastur, and heat protection with Mahila Housing Trust. (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/godigit_digitinsurance-heatinsurance-parametricinsurance-activity-7341758644490764288-StEd)

- WTW (Willis): Structures parametric programmes in Asia-Pacific that pay on defined triggers. Heat is a stated application; no specific Asian heat programme is documented yet. (https://www.wtwco.com/en-hk/solutions/services/parametric-solutions)

- Aon: Advises on parametric risk transfer, including temperature-triggered cover for heat delays and losses. Its published heat example is outside Asia. (https://www.aon.com/en/insights/articles/parametric-can-help-mitigate-extreme-heat-risks-for-contractors-in-emea)

- Marsh: Structures parametric cover in Asia using temperature, rainfall and water triggers, for example for data-centre disruption. (https://www.marsh.com/th/en/services/risk-consulting/insights/el-nino-climate-data-centre-business-interruption-asia.html)

- Munich Re: Reinsurer offering parametric and weather-risk solutions, including for heat and water stress affecting industry. (https://www.munichre.com/en/solutions/for-industry-clients/parametric-solutions.html)

- Hannover Re: Reinsurer that supports the Natural Disaster Fund and reports developing flood and heatwave covers. (https://www.hannover-re.com/1979241/sustainability-report-2022.pdf)

- SCOR: Reinsurer that helped develop Heat Stress Protect for dairy income; that heat case is outside Asia. (https://www.scor.com/en/news/launch-heat-stress-protect-insurance-protect-dairy-income-climate-change)

- General Insurance Corporation of India (GIC Re): India’s state reinsurer, backing crop and weather-based insurance schemes. A heat-income product is not confirmed. (https://www.gicre.in/en/business)

- HDFC ERGO General Insurance: Indian insurer with weather-index cover that uses rainfall and temperature indices. A worker heat-income product is not confirmed. (https://www.hdfcergo.com/commercial-insurance/weather-insurance)

- AXA Climate: Combines parametric insurance with climate science and adaptation advice, with teams in New Delhi, Hong Kong and Shanghai. A worker heat programme is not confirmed. (https://www.axa.com/commitments/axa-climate)

- MSIG (Mitsui Sumitomo Insurance): Offers parametric drought cover for farmers in Vietnam, powered by Hillridge, and has weather-index cover that includes heat stress in Australia. (https://www.msig-asia.com/sustainability)

- Tokio Marine Group: Japanese insurer supporting disaster risk schemes and parametric payouts. A heat-specific product is not confirmed. (https://www.tokiomarinehd.com/en/news_insights/ni42.html)

- Generali Global Corporate & Commercial: Provides underwriting capacity for parametric climate cover with Descartes. A specific Asian heat offering is not established. (https://www.generaliglobalcorporate.com/media/press-releases/all/2026/Descartes-and-Generali-Global-Corporate-Commercial-renew-long-term-strategic-partnership-to-reinforce-their-global-leadership-in-parametric-insurance.html)

- Descartes Underwriting: Parametric underwriter with explicit extreme-temperature cover for companies and public bodies. (https://descartesunderwriting.com/solutions/extreme-temperatures)

- Arbol: Builds parametric temperature and dairy heat-stress products; its high-temperature cover is US-focused. (https://www.arbol.io/products/temperature-risk-solutions)

- Weather Risk Management Services (WRMS): India-based climate risk specialist whose platform designs and runs parametric products with temperature triggers. A worker heat programme is not confirmed. (https://wrmsglobal.com/securisk/)

- Hillridge Technology: Connects farmers with weather-index underwriters, including high-temperature cover; powers MSIG’s drought cover in Vietnam. (https://www.hillridge.com.au/faqs)

- Raincoat: Climate insurance platform for event-based protection. A heat product is not confirmed. (https://www.raincoat.com/climate-insurance-101)

- Pula: Agricultural insurance specialist working across Africa and Asia, including index-based products. A standalone heat product is not confirmed. (https://www.pula-advisors.com/productsandservices)

- OKO: Crop insurance technology using satellite weather data and mobile channels, mainly in Africa. A heat product is not confirmed. (https://oko.finance/products/)

- ACRE Africa: Develops index microinsurance and climate information for smallholder farmers in Africa. A heat product is not confirmed. (https://www.acreafrica.com/downloads/acre-africa-profile.pdf)

- FloodFlash: Parametric flood specialist using property-level sensors. No heat product identified; listed as a model of sensor-triggered cover. (https://floodflash.co/parametric-underwriting-at-floodflash/)

### Banks, regulators and microfinance

- Monetary Authority of Singapore: Its 2020 environmental risk guidelines expect banks to assess physical climate risk, including through scenario analysis and stress tests. Its Singapore-Asia Taxonomy (2023) covers emission cuts only, so there are no criteria yet for finance that helps people adapt to heat. (https://www.mas.gov.sg/news/media-releases/2023/mas-launches-worlds-first-multi-sector-transition-taxonomy)

- Bank of Thailand: A 2023 policy statement asks banks to build environmental and climate risk into governance, strategy, risk management and disclosure. It has worked with the World Bank on assessing physical climate risk in Thai banks’ loan books. (https://www.bot.or.th/en/financial-innovation/sustainable-finance/green/FIPCS-internalizing_environmental_and_climate_change.html)

- Otoritas Jasa Keuangan (Financial Services Authority), Indonesia: Its climate risk guideline for banks (2024, refined in 2026) includes data on Indonesia’s physical climate hazards. A 2022 rule lets banks restructure loans for borrowers in areas it designates as disaster-hit: after the 2025 Sumatra floods, Rp12.58 trillion for 237,083 borrowers. Heat has not yet been designated. (https://ojk.go.id/en/Publikasi/Roadmap-dan-Pedoman/Perbankan/Pages/The-2026-Banking-Climate-Risk-Management-and-Scenario-Analysis-CRMS-Guideline.aspx)

- Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas: Since 2021, banks must check whether a borrower’s collateral or income is exposed to climate hazards. In areas under a state of calamity, banks can give borrowers up to six months’ grace with no interest on interest or penalties, longer for farm loans. It also eased rules for lenders in drought-hit areas during the 2015–16 El Niño. (https://www.philstar.com/business/2025/10/27/2482726/bsp-expands-calamity-relief-banks-borrowers)

- State Bank of Vietnam: Requires banks to assess environmental risk before lending to projects (since 2023). After Typhoon Yagi in 2024, it let lenders reschedule repayments for affected borrowers across 26 provinces, with final repayment allowed until the end of 2027. (https://vietnamnews.vn/economy/1688781/banks-allowed-to-extend-debt-repayment-for-typhoon-yagi-affected-customers-to-2027.html)

- Bangladesh Bank: Steers credit to farmers after climate shocks through its refinancing schemes. In June 2026 it told banks to prioritise farmers hit by heavy rain. Heat is not yet among the shocks that trigger this support. (https://www.bssnews.net/news/391823)

- Nepal Rastra Bank: Sets environmental and social risk rules for banks (2018), and since October 2024 a green finance taxonomy that sorts lending into green, amber and red. (https://www.sbfnetwork.org/wp-content/assets/policy-library/1440_Nepal_Guideline_on_ESRM_for_Banks_and_FIs_2018_NRB.pdf)

- Reserve Bank of India: Its 2018 directions let banks reschedule loans and pause repayments in areas hit by notified calamities, which in India now include heatwaves. A 2024 draft framework would require banks to disclose their climate-related financial risks. (https://rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_ViewMasDirections.aspx?id=10478)
