- Sustainable Banking and Finance Network: A network of financial regulators and banking associations from emerging markets, supported by IFC. Its policy library holds the climate and environmental risk rules of central banks across South and Southeast Asia. (https://www.sbfnetwork.org/)

- KOMIDA, with Build Change (Indonesia): One of Indonesia’s largest microfinance institutions, piloting small home-improvement loans for climate adaptation with Build Change, aimed at women earning under US$5 a day and paired with digital advice. (https://www.globalinnovation.fund/investments/build-change-2)

- Center for Financial Inclusion: Researches how small loans and parametric insurance can help low-income people get through heatwaves. (https://centerforfinancialinclusion.org/inclusive-finance-and-extreme-heat-how-small-loans-and-parametric-insurance-can-help-vulnerable-populations-manage-through-deadly-heat-waves)

### Philanthropy and funders

- Prudence Foundation: Funds heat-health early warnings for women informal workers in India, sent mainly over WhatsApp and reaching 50,000 women, and research with the Red Cross Red Crescent on heat, humidity and health. (https://www.prudentialplc.com/en/newsroom/company-news/2024/prudential-advances-climate-resilience-efforts-in-asia-and-africa-with-us-million-investment-to-address-impacts-of-climate-change-on-health/)

- Philanthropy Asia Alliance: Backs the Southeast Asia Heat Health Hub, the first regional hub of the Global Heat Health Information Network, and convenes funders on heat resilience. (https://www.eco-business.com/press-releases/philanthropy-asia-alliance-supports-southeast-asia-heat-health-hub-to-scale-coordinated-action-on-extreme-heat/)

- Temasek Trust (through Temasek Foundation): Its Liveability Challenge funds cooling innovations for extreme heat, such as passive cooling paints. (https://www.temasektrust.org.sg/what-we-do/impact-hub/article-details/the-liveability-challenge-2025-passive-cooling-hydrogen-storage-innovations)

- Rohini Nilekani Philanthropies: Funds heat work in India, including Prayas Energy and Health Group’s work with street vendors and construction workers, and CEEW’s district heat risk assessment. (https://rohininilekaniphilanthropies.org/resources/alliance-magazine-a-heat-justice-compass-for-philanthropic-action/)

- HT Parekh Foundation: Its flagship ReVIVE programme tackles urban heat in India’s smaller cities through research, cooling solutions, demonstration projects and policy advocacy. (https://indiaclimatecollaborative.org/blog/climate-funder-ht-parekh-foundation-on-heat)

- Rainmatter Foundation: Funds climate and environment work in India. Its partners’ heat work includes heatwave workshops that help journalists and health experts report on extreme heat. (https://rainmatter.org/blog/tag/heat/)

- Climate & Health Funders Coalition: Launched at COP30 with US$300 million in initial funding. Extreme heat is a core priority. Members include CIFF, the Gates Foundation, Philanthropy Asia Alliance, the Rockefeller Foundation and Wellcome. (https://wellcome.org/engagement-and-advocacy/advocacy-and-partnerships/climate-health-funders-coalition)

- Children’s Investment Fund Foundation: A member of the Climate & Health Funders Coalition, focused on the growing danger extreme heat poses to pregnant mothers, infants and children. (https://climateworks.org/press-release/statement-on-the-united-nations-secretary-generals-call-to-action-for-extreme-heat/)

- ClimateWorks Foundation: Its Adaptation & Resilience Fund made extreme heat its first focus, awarding US$9.3 million for parametric insurance, adaptive social protection, heat action plans and early warnings. (https://www.climateworks.org/blog/meet-the-grantees-from-our-global-call-for-extreme-heat-solutions/)

- The Rockefeller Foundation: Funds the South Asia Climate–Health Desk with Wellcome and a heat research consortium at IISER Pune, and supported C40’s Cool Cities Accelerator. (https://wmo.int/node/38332)

- Wellcome: Funds research on extreme heat and health: £17.5 million to test heat adaptations such as cool roofs, with a trial site in India; £17 million across nine projects on heat in pregnancy and early childhood; and work on heat and mental health. With The Rockefeller Foundation it committed US$11.5 million to the WHO–WMO Climate and Health Joint Programme. (https://wellcome.org/our-priorities/climate-and-health/extreme-heat)

- Laudes Foundation: Funds a three-year project with ICCCAD that builds Bangladeshi garment workers’ capacity on climate change, including heat stress, and on labour rights. (https://icccad.net/programmes/just-transition/capacitating-garment-workers/)

- International Development Research Centre (IDRC): Funds applied heat research, including gender-sensitive heat action planning in India and studies of heat’s impact on informal workers. (https://idrc-crdi.ca/en/what-we-do/projects-we-support/project/climate-adaptive-action-plans-manage-heat-stress-indian)

- IKEA Foundation: Supports solar-powered cooling that helps farmers preserve food and reduce waste as extreme heat becomes more common. (https://www.ikeafoundation.org/campaign-26)

- Swiss Capacity Building Facility (SCBF): Supports inclusive financial services, including income protection against extreme heat and rainfall for women in India’s informal sector. (https://www.scbf.ch/projects?665a6c47_page=2)

- Howden Foundation: Funds HERA’s work in India combining early warnings, direct cash and parametric insurance for women exposed to extreme heat. (https://www.howdenfoundation.com/news/frontline-voices-her-resilience-india)

- India Climate Collaborative: Connects philanthropy, researchers and practitioners on heat resilience, sharing evidence on implementation gaps, worker protection and financing. (https://indiaclimatecollaborative.org/blog/mumbai-climate-week-through-conversations-on-urban-resilience)

- Clean Cooling Collaborative (ClimateWorks Foundation): Mobilises philanthropy for efficient, climate-friendly cooling, including access to cooling and passive design. (https://www.cleancoolingcollaborative.org/)

- Novo Nordisk Foundation: Its Nexa Lighthouse call funds protection from heat for people with heart and metabolic diseases in South Asia (open until 17 November 2026), and a 2027 challenge programme on heat and hypertension. (https://novonordiskfonden.dk/en/grant/nexa-lighthouse-call-protecting-people-with-cardiometabolic-diseases-from-the-impacts-of-heat-in-south-asia/)

- EarthON Foundation: Its Greenovation challenge gives awards to Indian ventures for cool roofs, passive and community cooling, and heat-safe livelihoods. (https://earthonfoundation.org/greenovation-urban-climate-resilience-challenge/)

- Ramboll Foundation: Funds urban heat tools and research, including a DKK 1.18 million grant for an urban heat and flooding tool and radiant-cooling research. Funding for Asian applicants is not confirmed. (https://www.ramboll.com/news/unep-cop30-presidency-and-ramboll-partner-to-tackle-the-threat-of-urban-heating)

- National Research Foundation, Singapore: Funds Project HeatSafe, which studies heat, health and productivity among workers in Singapore and partner countries including Vietnam and Cambodia, and Cooling Singapore. (https://medicine.nus.edu.sg/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/PRESS-RELEASE_Project-HeatSafe-18MAR2024-FOR-IMMEDIATE-RELEASE.pdf)

- Research Grants Council, Hong Kong: Has funded community heat-risk planning and, in 2025, real-time heat-health warnings for older adults in Hong Kong. (https://www.cuhk.edu.hk/research/SED/Projects/Research_b2_health%20risk.html)

- Research Council of Norway: Co-funds COPE, a research project building early warnings for combined heat and air pollution in Delhi and Kolkata. (https://www.cicero.oslo.no/en/articles/will-develop-advanced-early-warning-and-decision-support-systems-for-heat-and-air-pollution-delhi-and-kolkata)

- U.S. National Science Foundation: A named co-funder of COPE, the four-year heat and air-pollution early warning research project in Delhi and Kolkata. (https://www.cicero.oslo.no/en/articles/will-develop-advanced-early-warning-and-decision-support-systems-for-heat-and-air-pollution-delhi-and-kolkata)

- Asia-Pacific Network for Global Change Research (APN): Funds regional research and capacity building, including a US$40,000 grant for gender-sensitive heat action policies in South Asia and newer work on urban heat in Southeast Asian cities. (https://www.apn-gcr.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/CBA2021-07SY-Magotra-Final-Report-_APN.docx-1.pdf)

- National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR): Funds HEAT-PROTECT in Andhra Pradesh (2023–2027), building heat adaptation into primary healthcare for vulnerable groups. (https://ghrcentre-ncdec.nihr.ac.uk/project/heat-exposure-adaptation-tools-protecting-vulnerable-g/)

- Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR): Funds medical research including a 2025 study of heat-health risk communication among construction workers, manual labourers and street vendors. (https://smcw.edu.in/assets/pdf/2025/Extramural%20Funded%20Research%20Projects.pdf)

- Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF): Runs a joint 2026 call with India’s Ministry of Earth Sciences on mountain hazards that explicitly covers heatwaves and their links to forests and horticulture. (https://www.snf.ch/media/en/sMJbvJyKnKsYuNTK/call_doc_SNSF-MoES_2026.pdf)

- Ministry of Earth Sciences, Government of India: Funds the Indian side of the 2026 Indo-Swiss mountain-hazards research call, which includes how heatwaves are changing. (https://www.snf.ch/media/en/sMJbvJyKnKsYuNTK/call_doc_SNSF-MoES_2026.pdf)

- Department of Science and Technology, Government of India: Funds research on low-energy cooling and better building envelopes, and backed the Global Cooling Prize, whose winners were announced in 2021. (https://dst.gov.in/building-energy-efficiency-research-initiative-beri)

- Higher Education Commission, Pakistan: Funded heat-resistant soybean breeding at the University of Agriculture Faisalabad (2022–2025), with a demonstration running to 2027. (https://web.uaf.edu.pk/UploadFiles/UAFAnualReport/4381f032-04fb-4a85-9f2d-8e0adc426a54.pdf)

- The Lemelson Foundation: Supported the Global Cooling Prize, which in 2021 rewarded room air conditioners with far lower climate impact, aimed first at India. (https://www.lemelson.org/winners-of-the-global-cooling-prize-announced/)

- The Hong Kong Jockey Club Charities Trust: Funds the three-year Jockey Club Beat the Heat project (from 2024), which assesses risk and gives personal protection and community support to vulnerable older people in Hong Kong. (https://www.cpr.cuhk.edu.hk/en/press/jockey-club-beat-the-heat-project-helps-elderly-stay-safe-and-healthy-during-extreme-heat/)

- Poul Due Jensen Foundation (Grundfos Foundation): Funds water access, including €120,000 for urban poor communities in the Philippines. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://www.pdjf.dk/en/article/new-community-engagement-grants-march-2025/)

- Robert Bosch Stiftung: Supports quick, community-led adaptation grants through the Climate Communities Adaptation Facility, and work on climate and migration. Heat-specific funding in Asia is not confirmed. (https://bosch-stiftung.de/en/story/climate-mobility-times-global-upheaval)

- A.T.E. Chandra Foundation: Funds the revival of village waterbodies with communities, NGOs and government, starting in drought-hit Marathwada and now in 11 Indian states. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://www.atecf.org/water-and-agriculture)

- DCM Shriram Foundation: Funds watershed work in Rajasthan with Tarun Bharat Sangh and an AgWater challenge on farm water use and farmer resilience. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://www.dcmshriramfoundation.org/programs/khushali-paryavaran)

- Cipla Foundation: Funds watershed partnerships with MYRADA and BAIF in five Indian states, with water-user groups that maintain the structures. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://www.cipla.com/csr/cipla-foundation/environmental-sustainability.html)

- Dharampal Satyapal Limited (DS Group) CSR: Funds Water Economic Zones in Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh through local partners. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://www.dsgroup.com/front/img/disclosures/List-of-Projects/List%20of%20Projects%202025-26.pdf)

- HDFC Life (Swabhimaan CSR): Funds city forests and waterbody revival in Sikkim, Maharashtra and Gujarat alongside livelihoods and health work. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://www.hdfclife.com/hdfc-careers/csr.html)

- CIMB Foundation: Gives grants to registered organisations working with Malaysian communities, including a gravity-fed water programme in Sabah; applications are accepted October to December. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://www.cimbfoundation.com/collaborate-with-us/grant-application-form.html)

- Yayasan PETRONAS: Funds community-based disaster risk management in Malaysia through implementing partners. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://www.yayasanpetronas.com.my/request-for-proposal-community-based-disaster-risk-management-cbdrm/)

- Nusantara Fund (Dana Nusantara): Funds Indigenous peoples and local communities in Indonesia directly, such as protecting water sources in Central Sulawesi. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://nusantarafund.org/en/program/mosintuwu-community/)

- Women’s Fund Asia: Gives flexible and core grants to women-led and feminist groups in 22 Asian countries and territories, covering labour rights, environmental justice and women-led climate adaptation. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://www.womensfundasia.org/strengthening-feminist-movements/)

- Tewa, Nepal Women’s Fund: Makes small grants to grassroots women’s groups in Nepal; one won municipal funding for irrigation after training on climate budgets. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://annualreport.bothends.org/nepalese-women-lead-local-advocacy-on-climate-change/)

- Mama Cash: A participatory funder of feminist movements and a member of GAGGA, which gives core, multi-year funding to women-led community groups, including in Nepal, India and Indonesia. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://www.mamacash.org/resources/our-agenda-at-cop30-scaling-up-funding-for-feminist-locally-led-adaptation/)

- Both ENDS: Supports environmental-justice partners, including grants for local climate governance and gender budgeting in Nepal. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://prc.org.np/publications/)

- Global Fund for Community Foundations: Funds community philanthropy and local funds in India, Nepal, Indonesia, the Philippines and Cambodia, including climate resilience. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://globalfundcommunityfoundations.org/what-we-do/grants/grants-awarded/)

- DOEN Foundation: Co-funded the 2022 Global LEAP Off-Grid Cold Chain Challenge, which included Indian finalists keeping produce cool off the grid. (https://efficiencyforaccess.org/updates/global-leap-awards-announces-winners-and-finalists-of-the-2022-off-grid-cold-chain-challenge/)

- Good Energies Foundation: Co-funded the 2022 Global LEAP Off-Grid Cold Chain Challenge, which included Indian finalists keeping produce cool off the grid. (https://efficiencyforaccess.org/updates/global-leap-awards-announces-winners-and-finalists-of-the-2022-off-grid-cold-chain-challenge/)

- Henry Luce Foundation: Gave US$945,000 in 2022 for research on vulnerable deltas in Southeast Asia: climate, water pollution and social change. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://hluce.org/new-lucesea-grants-address-growing-impact-climate-change-and-importance-community-histories/)

- MetLife Foundation: Gave US$120,000 to WWF Nepal’s JEEWAN project in Bardiya, combining new livelihoods with nature-based flood protection. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://www.metlife.com.np/content/dam/metlifecom/np/homepage/en/about-metlife/media-downloads/pres-release/press-articles/MetLife_Foundation_Supports_WWF_JEEWAN_Project.pdf)

- Stone Family Foundation: Finances household water services in Cambodia, with grants, loans and technical support for water operators. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://www.stonefamilyfoundation.org.uk/water-to-the-home/who-we-work-with/)

- The Waterloo Foundation: Funds reliable safe water in Nepal’s schools and the upkeep of water services. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://waterloofoundation.org.uk/world-development-water-and-sanitation-small-projects-supported/)

- Fondation SUEZ: Funds access to water, sanitation and hygiene, with India, Bangladesh and the Philippines among eligible countries. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://56q2bbylxfnk.optimytool.com/fr)

- Halton Foundation: Gives research grants of up to US$30,000 a year on indoor environments, explicitly including thermal comfort, with no geographic limits. The next round opens 1 July 2027. (https://foundation.halton.com/)

- Takeda (Global CSR Program): Funds climate-resilient health systems, including about US$7.1 million with UNOPS in Bangladesh and US$8.4 million with Vitamin Angels in Indonesia. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://www.takeda.com/newsroom/newsreleases/2025/takeda-employees-vote-csr-collaborations/)

- Danone Communities: Invests patiently in affordable drinking-water enterprises such as Naandi Community Water Services in India. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://www.danonecommunities.com/naandi-community-water-services/)

- Fondation Botnar: Funds Urban Futures, linking young people’s wellbeing and climate-resilient food systems in intermediary cities, including in Indonesia. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://www.fondationbotnar.org/project/urban-futures/)

- OPEC Fund for International Development: Lends and gives technical assistance for water security and services in Asia, including US$100 million for water security in Sri Lanka in 2025. Heat-specific funding is not confirmed. (https://www.adb.org/who-we-are/partners/ofid/overview)

## Extreme heat in twelve Asian cities

What extreme heat is doing in 12 Asian cities: whether each has a heat plan, the vicious cycles the evidence ties to it, who is hit hardest and who is already at work.

### Singapore, Singapore

A city-state with hot nights, dense towers and an early national heat stress advisory.

Heat action plan (Heat plan in force): Singapore launched a national Heat Stress Advisory in July 2023. It rates heat stress as low, moderate or high from the wet-bulb globe temperature, and tells people what to do at each level. Sources: Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment, 2023 https://mse.gov.sg/latest-news/press-release-heat-stress-advisory

- The sleepless-nights loop: Singapore has averaged 76 warm nights a year over four decades; by 2100 they could come on most nights.

- The cooling trap: The commercial centre has measured up to about 7 °C warmer than the outskirts on calm, clear nights.

- The dying-green loop: Among the cities where the most urban tree species already face temperatures beyond their range.

- The invisible-deaths loop: Workplace monitors found more heat stress than nearby weather stations reported.

Who heat hits hardest: Workers in heat-exposed jobs; Older people

Already at work: National Environment Agency, Singapore; Ministry of Manpower, Singapore; Singapore Management University, Urban Institute; National Research Foundation, Singapore; Monetary Authority of Singapore; C40 Cities

Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/singapore/

### Bangkok, Thailand

A tropical megacity where heat costs lives, livelihoods and a share of the city’s economy.

Heat action plan (Heat plan in force): For the 2026 hot season Bangkok opened 304 cooling centres in schools, health centres and district offices, under a heat management plan developed with the World Bank. Sources: Government of Thailand, 2026 https://thailand.go.th/issue-focus-detail/bangkok-launches-304-cooling-centers-to-combat-extreme-heat; World Bank, Shaping a Cooler Bangkok, 2025 https://www.worldbank.org/en/country/thailand/publication/shaping-a-cooler-bangkok-tackling-urban-heat-for-a-more-livable-city

- The poverty–heat trap: Nearly 80% of informal workers surveyed cut their hours in the heat; 75% of home-based workers lost a day’s work a month to heat illness.

- The reactive-spending loop: Heat deaths, about 593 a year, cost up to 0.7% of the city’s economy: more than its 2020 public health budget.

- The sleepless-nights loop: One of the tropical cities whose nights stay hot.

- The green-displacement loop: Fieldwork is tracing how green urban renewal affects the city’s lower-income residents.

Who heat hits hardest: Workers in heat-exposed jobs; People in informal settlements

Already at work: HomeNet Thailand; Bank of Thailand; United Nations Development Programme (UNDP); Asian Development Bank

Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/bangkok/

### Hanoi, Vietnam

A fast-growing northern capital whose power and water strain together in the heat.

Heat action plan (No published city heat plan found): No city heat action plan found. From 2018 to 2021 the Viet Nam Red Cross ran an early-action plan for heatwaves in 15 of Hanoi’s wards, triggered by a heat-index forecast. Sources: Anticipation Hub https://www.anticipation-hub.org/experience/anticipatory-action-in-the-world/vietnam/fbf-ready-reducing-heat-waves-impacts-on-the-vulnerable-populations-of-hanoi

- The energy–water loop: In May and June 2023 heat drove demand up as hydropower reservoirs ran low; blackouts in the north cost about US$1.4 billion.

- The global cooling loop: Southeast Asia’s air conditioners could rise from 40 million to 300 million by 2040.

Who heat hits hardest: Workers in heat-exposed jobs

Already at work: State Bank of Vietnam

Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/hanoi/

### Manila, Philippines

A dense, humid metropolis where heat closes schools and pushes the heat index into danger.

Heat action plan (Parts in place, no full plan found): In Metro Manila, Quezon City has set up a city Heat Action Team, named chief heat action officers and opened 32 libraries as cooling centres. Its full heat action plan is still being developed. Sources: Quezon City Government https://quezoncity.gov.ph/qc-beefs-up-action-vs-extreme-heat-designates-chief-heat-action-officers/

- The lost-schooling loop: In April 2024, 5,288 schools in the Philippines moved to remote learning, affecting more than 3.6 million students.

- The cooling trap: One of the dense, high-rise city cores where air-conditioner waste heat adds to the night.

- The farm-debt loop: Rice yields in the Philippines fell about 10% for each 1 °C rise in growing-season night temperature.

Who heat hits hardest: Workers in heat-exposed jobs; People in informal settlements

Already at work: PAGASA, Philippines; Department of Education, Philippines

Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/manila/

### Jakarta, Indonesia

A sinking, sprawling capital in the country where half of Southeast Asia’s air conditioners could be.

Heat action plan (Parts in place, no full plan found): No standalone heat action plan found. Jakarta’s Climate Action Plan 2021–2050 aims to reduce its vulnerability to extreme heat, and in October 2025 the governor told health facilities to prepare for heat illness. Sources: C40 Cities, 2025 https://www.c40.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/RfP_RF_Jakarta.pdf; Antara, 2025 https://www.antaranews.com/berita/5178905/pramono-instruksikan-mitigasi-dampak-cuaca-panas-ekstrem-di-jakarta

- The global cooling loop: Half of Southeast Asia’s projected 300 million air conditioners in 2040 could be in Indonesia.

- The wildfire loop: Indonesia’s 2015 forest and peat fires cost an estimated US$16.1 billion.

- The dying-green loop: Among the hot, fast-growing cities where urban trees are at risk.

Who heat hits hardest: People in informal settlements; Workers in heat-exposed jobs

Already at work: Otoritas Jasa Keuangan (Financial Services Authority), Indonesia; KOMIDA, with Build Change (Indonesia); Nusantara Fund (Dana Nusantara)

Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/jakarta/

### Delhi, India

A capital of extreme pre-monsoon heat, street trade and falling groundwater.

Heat action plan (Heat plan in force): Delhi launched its 2025 Heat Action Plan in April 2025, with graded heat alerts, cooling shelters, 3,000 water points and heatstroke units in hospitals. Experts have recommended legal backing and dedicated funds to strengthen it. Sources: Business Today, 2025 https://www.businesstoday.in/amp/india/story/imd-predicts-heatwave-conditions-in-april-delhi-govt-launches-action-plan-472890-2025-04-21; Citizen Matters https://citizenmatters.in/city-buzz-five-things-you-must-know-about-the-delhi-heat-action-plan

- The heat credit squeeze: Of 721 Delhi street vendors surveyed in 2024, 80% saw fewer customers in heatwaves and 49% lost income.

- The dying-green loop: New Delhi is among the cities where every urban tree species studied is at risk from rising heat.

- The groundwater loop: North-west India (Rajasthan, Punjab and Haryana) lost 109 km³ of groundwater in six years, mainly to irrigation.

- The invisible-deaths loop: India confirmed 185 heatstroke deaths against 48,385 suspected cases in 2024, up to 28 July.

Who heat hits hardest: Workers in heat-exposed jobs; People in informal settlements

Already at work: National Disaster Management Authority, India; India Meteorological Department and IITM Pune; National Centre for Disease Control, India; Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW); SEEDS; HeatWatch India

Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/delhi/

### Dhaka, Bangladesh

One of the world’s densest cities, where heat costs workdays and fills tin-roofed homes.

Heat action plan (Parts in place, no full plan found): Dhaka North City Corporation appointed Asia’s first Chief Heat Officer in 2023. No city heat action plan found yet. Sources: Arsht-Rock Resilience Center, 2023 https://onebillionresilient.org/2023/05/03/bushra-afreen-dhaka-chief-heat-officer/

- The poverty–heat trap: Heat-related illness cost Bangladesh 250 million workdays in 2024, worth up to US$1.78 billion.

- The energy-poverty trap: Tin-roofed informal settlements trap heat for people who can’t afford to cool.

- The displacement loop: Migrants land in settlements on the edges of the city, often in heat-trapping housing.

- The lost-schooling loop: Bangladesh closed schools for about 33 million children in its April 2024 heatwave.

Who heat hits hardest: Workers in heat-exposed jobs; People in informal settlements

Already at work: Dhaka North City Corporation; Bangladesh Red Crescent Society; icddr,b; BRAC; Practical Action; Bangladesh Bank

Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/dhaka/

### Kathmandu, Nepal

A valley city warming fast, below the Himalayan ice that feeds South Asia’s rivers.

Heat action plan (No published city heat plan found): No city heat action plan found. Nepal adopted a national plan of action on heat waves in 2024, and Nepalgunj, in the plains, wrote the country’s first local heat action plan in 2023. Sources: Onlinekhabar, 2025 https://english.onlinekhabar.com/reassessing-nepals-heat-wave-response-lessons-from-2024-and-the-way-forward.html; Nepalgunj Heat Action Plan, 2023 https://preparecenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/Nepalgunj-Heat-Action-Plan-2023.pdf

- The melting-ice loop: The Hindu Kush Himalaya’s glaciers lost ice 65% faster in the 2010s, and could lose 30–50% of their volume by 2100.

- The medical-debt trap: In five cities in Nepal and Bangladesh, heat cut incomes and pushed some households towards high-interest loans.

Who heat hits hardest: Women whose livelihoods are held back by unequal access; Older people

Already at work: National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, Nepal; Nepal Red Cross Society; Tewa, Nepal Women’s Fund; Nepal Rastra Bank; Practical Action

Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/kathmandu/

### Mumbai, India

A coastal megacity where the nights are heating faster than the days.

Heat action plan (Parts in place, no full plan found): Mumbai’s 2022 Climate Action Plan names urban heat as a priority, and the city is working with C40 on heat-health protocols for its hospitals. No standalone city heat action plan found. Sources: Citizen Matters https://citizenmatters.in/mcap-climate-change-heat-mumbai/; C40 Cities, 2026 https://www.c40.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/RfP-Heat-Health-protocols-for-Mumbai.pdf

- The sleepless-nights loop: Mumbai gained 15 very warm nights a summer over the last decade.

- The energy-poverty trap: Tin-roofed informal settlements trap heat for people who can’t afford to cool.

- The invisible-deaths loop: Death certificates usually record the immediate cause, so heat as the trigger goes unrecorded.

Who heat hits hardest: People in informal settlements; Workers in heat-exposed jobs

Already at work: WRI India; C40 Cities; HDFC Life (Swabhimaan CSR); ICLEI South Asia

Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/mumbai/

### Ahmedabad, India

Where South Asia’s first heat action plan began, and where its results were measured.

Heat action plan (Heat plan in force): Ahmedabad launched South Asia’s first heat action plan in 2013, after a 2010 heatwave caused an estimated 1,344 excess deaths. An estimated 1,190 deaths a year were later avoided. Sources: Hess et al., Journal of Environmental and Public Health, 2018 https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6236972/

- The overwhelmed-clinic loop: The plan prepared hospitals and warned the public before heat peaked.

- The poverty–heat trap: Up to three-quarters of India’s workforce depends on heat-exposed work.

- The invisible-deaths loop: As in most countries, heat deaths are hard to count, which makes the case for prevention harder to see.

Who heat hits hardest: Workers in heat-exposed jobs; People in informal settlements

Already at work: Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, with IIPH Gandhinagar and NRDC; All India Disaster Mitigation Institute (AIDMI); IBISA; C40 Cities; Heat Resilience Action (HERA), formerly Climate Resilience for All

Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/ahmedabad/

### Colombo, Sri Lanka

A coastal capital where humid heat meets crowded markets, harbours and fish landing sites.

Heat action plan (Parts in place, no full plan found): Colombo Municipal Council, with the Department of Meteorology and SLYCAN Trust, has worked on guidelines for a gender-sensitive heat action plan. The Department of Meteorology issues heat index advisories. No adopted city heat plan found yet. Sources: APN and SLYCAN Trust, 2022 https://www.apn-gcr.org/publication/colombo-municipal-council-sri-lanka-integrating-heat-stress-management-into-climate-policies-and-guidelines-for-gender-sensitive-heat-action-plans-in-sri-lanka/; News 1st, 2024 https://english.newsfirst.lk/2024/03/04/heat-advisory-issued-by-sri-lanka-s-met-dept

- The cooling trap: A University of Colombo study found a pronounced urban heat island, as green space gives way to concrete and asphalt.

- The poverty–heat trap: Heat advisories ask people to work in the shade; market and fish workers who sell in the open often cannot.

Who heat hits hardest: Workers in heat-exposed jobs; Coastal and riverine communities

Already at work: Asia-Pacific Network for Global Change Research (APN); World Meteorological Organization; UN ESCAP

Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/colombo/

### Phnom Penh, Cambodia

A fast-growing capital of garment factories and metal roofs, where the hot season peaks before the rains.

Heat action plan (No published city heat plan found): A proposal with the Ministry of Water Resources and Meteorology and Phnom Penh Capital Hall would develop a heat action plan for the city, with thresholds and response protocols. No adopted city heat plan found yet. Sources: National Committee for Sub-National Democratic Development https://library.ncdd.gov.kh/detail/17224/download

- The cooling trap: UN ESCAP projects that the urban heat island could add 2 °C to 7 °C on top of global warming in Phnom Penh.

- The poverty–heat trap: At three garment factories, workers reporting heat symptoms rose from 68% in the cooler months to 88% in the hot months.

- The lost-schooling loop: In the April 2024 heatwave, Cambodia shortened public school days by two hours.

Who heat hits hardest: Workers in heat-exposed jobs; People in informal settlements

Already at work: UN ESCAP; Asian Development Bank; World Bank

Page: https://beattheheat.asia/cities/phnompenh/

## Heatwaves that shaped South and Southeast Asia, 1998 to 2026

10 major heatwaves across South and Southeast Asia, from Odisha in 1998 to 2026: what happened, what it cost and what changed afterwards. Recorded deaths are a floor, not a total: many heat deaths are never counted as heat deaths. Where no solid count exists, the timeline says so.

### May 1998, Odisha, India: The heatwave that taught Odisha to plan

Peak: Coastal Odisha, not known for extreme heat. Toll: 2,042 deaths from heatstroke recorded by hospitals.

Heat struck a coastal state that had never planned for it, and hospitals counted more than two thousand heatstroke deaths in a single month.

What changed: Odisha wrote its first heat action plan in 1999. The next year, recorded heat deaths fell to 91.

Source: Down To Earth: how to fight heat wave the Odisha way https://www.downtoearth.org.in/environment/how-to-fight-heat-wave-the-odisha-way-49950

### May–June 2003, Andhra Pradesh, India: Three weeks that killed more than 1,300

Peak: Weeks of heat across the state. Toll: 1,317 deaths in Andhra Pradesh in three weeks, as reported then.

A long spell of heat before the monsoon killed more than 1,300 people in Andhra Pradesh in three weeks.

What changed: The same region would be hit again, even harder, in 2015.

Source: The Tribune, 8 June 2003 https://www.tribuneindia.com/2003/20030608/main6.htm

### May 2010, Ahmedabad, India: The heatwave behind South Asia’s first city heat plan

Peak: 46.8 °C. Toll: An estimated 1,344 excess deaths, 43% more than in the same weeks of 2009 and 2011.

The toll was measured as excess deaths: the deaths above normal for those weeks, found by comparing death records with other years.

What changed: In 2013 Ahmedabad launched South Asia’s first heat action plan: early warnings, prepared hospitals and outreach. An estimated 1,190 deaths a year were later avoided.

Source: Hess et al., Journal of Environmental and Public Health, 2018 https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6236972/

### May–June 2015, India and Pakistan: South Asia’s deadliest recent heatwave

Peak: 40–45 °C for weeks in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. Toll: More than 2,500 deaths in India, mostly in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, and more than 1,100 in Pakistan, centred on Karachi.

Heat swept India’s south-east in May, then struck Karachi in June.

What changed: In the years after, Indian states and cities wrote dozens of heat action plans, and a 2023 review of 37 found that most had yet to secure funding or a vulnerability assessment.

Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica: India–Pakistan heat wave of 2015 https://www.britannica.com/print/article/2028529

Source: Centre for Policy Research, 2023: how is India adapting to heatwaves? https://cprindia.org/briefsreports/how-is-india-adapting-to-heatwaves-an-assessment-of-heat-action-plans-with-insights-for-transformative-climate-action/

### April 2016, Thailand and mainland Southeast Asia: El Niño and warming break Southeast Asia’s records

Peak: 44.6 °C at Mae Hong Son, Thailand’s highest ever at the time. Toll: No regional death count.

A strong El Niño drove record heat across mainland Southeast Asia. Researchers found El Niño caused about half of the extra warmth and global warming about a third.

What changed: The researchers found that since 1980 every April after an El Niño has set a new temperature record in the region.

Source: NASA Earth Observatory, 2016 https://earthobservatory.nasa.gov/NaturalHazards/view.php?id=87981

Source: University of Texas Institute for Geophysics, on Thirumalai et al., Nature Communications, 2017 https://www.jsg.utexas.edu/news/2017/06/scientists-unravel-how-el-nino-and-global-warming-combine-to-cause-record-breaking-heat-in-southeast-asia/

### March–April 2022, India and Pakistan: The spring that came months too hot

Peak: 49 °C in Pakistan; India’s hottest March in 122 years. Toll: At least 90 deaths reported.

Heat arrived in March, before the wheat was ready. Yields fell by an estimated 10–35% in Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Punjab, and power cuts and forest fires followed.

What changed: Scientists found climate change made it about 30 times more likely, and about 1 °C hotter.

Source: World Meteorological Organization, 2022: climate change made the heatwave 30 times more likely https://public.wmo.int/node/14883

Source: Carbon Brief, 2022 https://www.carbonbrief.org/climate-change-made-india-and-pakistans-2022-early-heatwave-30-times-more-likely

### April 2023, Bangladesh, India, Laos and Thailand: Humid heat that was near impossible without climate change

Peak: 45.4 °C at Tak, Thailand’s highest ever. Toll: No regional death count.

The heat index passed the dangerous 41 °C mark across large parts of South and Southeast Asia. In Bangladesh and India such humid heat used to come less than once a century; it can now be expected about every five years.

What changed: Scientists found it at least 30 times more likely because of climate change, and the heat in Laos and Thailand virtually impossible without it.

Source: World Weather Attribution, 2023 https://www.worldweatherattribution.org/?p=1870

Source: Yale Environment 360, 2023 https://e360.yale.edu/digest/april-2023-heat-wave-india-thailand-climate-change

### April 2024, South and Southeast Asia: Asia’s hottest April: schools shut from Dhaka to Manila

Peak: 48.2 °C at Chauk, Myanmar’s highest April temperature on record. Toll: At least 28 heat deaths reported in Bangladesh in April; likely an undercount.

Bangladesh closed schools for about 33 million children and the Philippines moved 5,288 schools to remote learning. In South Asia, a 30-day heatwave like it became about 45 times more likely.

What changed: Scientists found climate change made it about 1 °C hotter. Surges in heat deaths were also reported in Thailand and the Philippines.

Source: World Weather Attribution, reported by Down To Earth, 2024 https://www.downtoearth.org.in/news/climate-change/climate-change-responsible-for-over-80-of-temperature-rise-within-asia-last-month-the-hottest-april-ever-wwa-96153

Source: Borneo Post (AFP), 2024: Myanmar records 48.2 °C https://www.theborneopost.com/2024/04/30/myanmar-records-hottest-ever-april-temperature-of-48-2c/

Source: NBC News, 2024: school closures in the Philippines and Bangladesh https://www.nbcnews.com/news/world/schools-close-extreme-heat-philippines-bangladesh-asia-rcna149485

### May–June 2024, Northern India: The election heatwave

Peak: Nearly 50 °C in parts of the north; Delhi’s hottest night in more than five decades. Toll: 110 heat deaths and more than 40,000 suspected heatstroke cases officially recorded from 1 March to 18 June.

On the final day of voting, 33 polling staff died of heat in Uttar Pradesh alone. Official counts kept rising for weeks as states reported in.

What changed: Central government hospitals were told to set up heatwave units. Officials said the real toll was expected to be higher.

Source: The Tribune (PTI), 2024: 110 deaths, 40,000 suspected heatstroke cases https://www.tribuneindia.com/news/india/india-reports-110-deaths-40-000-heatstroke-cases-this-summer-632500/amp

Source: AFP via Malay Mail, 2 June 2024 https://www.malaymail.com/amp/news/world/2024/06/02/heatstroke-killed-33-indian-polling-staff-on-last-voting-day-says-state-election-chief/137732

### April 2026, India and Pakistan: A pre-monsoon heatwave made three times more likely

Peak: Above 46 °C in many cities. Toll: At least 37 heat deaths reported in India and 10 in Karachi; likely undercounted.

Fifteen days of heat in late April pushed India’s electricity demand to a record and brought farm drought to more than a million square kilometres.

What changed: Scientists found April heat like this now returns about every five years.

Source: World Weather Attribution, 2026 https://www.worldweatherattribution.org/climate-change-exposes-hundreds-of-millions-to-longer-and-deadlier-pre-monsoon-heat-in-south-asia/

Source: Mongabay, 2026 https://news.mongabay.com/short-article/2026/05/climate-change-triples-chance-of-deadly-2026-south-asia-pre-monsoon-heatwave-report/

## Practical actions against extreme heat, by setting

34 practical actions against extreme heat in workplaces, homes, schools, health facilities, markets and neighbourhoods, and what municipalities can do before summer. Each answers eight questions: what to do, who it protects, where it suits, who must act, what it takes to run, the evidence, what could stop it, and what it only works with.

### Outdoor and hot workplaces

People who cannot stop working when it is hot: builders, vendors, riders, farm, factory and sanitation workers.

What workers told researchers: Stopping work means losing income; There is nowhere to recover; Safe drinking water costs too much; Home stays hot after the shift; Warnings don’t reach us in a useful way; No one local to install or fix it (People’s Courage International: Hot Cities Make Hard Work Harder, a study with workers in Delhi, Kathmandu, Dhaka, Jakarta and Quezon City, https://www.ccacoalition.org/events/hot-cities-make-hard-work-harder-strengthening-health-and-livelihood-resilience-informal-workers-south-and-southeast-asian-cities)

#### Worker cooling stations

Evidence: Reported, not evaluated · Before the season

- What to do: Rest points where workers already are, with shade or cooling, seating, drinking water, rehydration salts, a first-aid kit and a way to reach a clinic.

- Who it protects: Construction workers, vendors, drivers, porters and loaders between jobs or on breaks.

- Where it suits: Construction sites, markets, bus and taxi stands, labour chowks and community spaces with heavy foot traffic.

- Who must act: City and local governments, Employers and businesses, Community and civil society groups

- Running and upkeep: Water, ice and salts every day; cleaning; power for fans; someone on site; repairs before each season.

- Evidence: The Migrants Resilience Collaborative reported that more than 27,000 workers used its cooling stations in India, Nepal and Bangladesh in one summer. These are the programme’s own figures; health and income effects have not been independently measured. (People’s Courage International, 2025: emergency response to the heatwave crisis in South and Southeast Asia, https://www.peoplescourageinternational.org/pdfs/Emergency%20response%20to%20heat%20wave%20crisis%20in%20South%20and%20Southeast%20Asia.pdf)

- What could stop it: A station nobody can leave work to use, or one that closes when the day is hottest.

- Works only if: Employers let workers use it without losing pay; It is open when people work; Someone refills and repairs it every day.

- Delivery, where: On the routes workers really use, not where land happens to be free

- Delivery, opening hours: Matched to working hours, including early mornings and evenings

- Delivery, services: Shade or cooling, safe water, seating, first aid, referral to a clinic

- Delivery, run by: A named person who checks, cleans, refills and repairs it

- Delivery, access barriers: Lost wages, permission to leave work, disability access, who feels welcome

- Delivery, how you will know: Visits, days open, user views, and health or income outcomes measured properly

Where it has been tried (Reported, not evaluated): At a Bengaluru construction site, a station cooled with water-soaked khus panels drew about 100–120 workers a day in April, falling to 70–80 after the monsoon began. (The Migration Story, https://themigrationstory.com/?p=19496)

Where it has been tried (Reported, not evaluated): In 2026, People’s Courage International ran 20 cooling centres in big cities, placed near construction sites, road junctions and the labour nakas where day-wage workers look for jobs, with water, rehydration salts and phone charging. It reported more than 88,000 visits, and up to 1,841 in a day at one centre. These are the programme’s own figures. (World Economic Forum and BCG, Workforce Heat Resilience: An Actionable Framework to Close the Execution Gap, 2026, https://www.weforum.org/publications/workforce-heat-resilience-an-actionable-framework-to-close-the-execution-gap/)

#### Warnings that reach workers

Evidence: Reported, not evaluated · During the heat

- What to do: Route official alerts through trusted worker messengers, voice notes and picture boards at stalls and labour chowks, with one clear action in each message and a way to report back.

- Who it protects: Vendors, labourers and anyone without a smartphone, signal or the time to read.

- Where it suits: Markets, labour chowks and worker unions or associations with leaders people trust.

- Who must act: Weather and climate services, Worker organisations and unions, Community and civil society groups

- Running and upkeep: A messenger’s time every alert day, printed boards, and someone who answers when workers report a problem.

- Evidence: In Delhi in 2025, the India Meteorological Department, worker organisations and Greenpeace India set up colour-coded heat boards at vending carts and sent bilingual audio and text alerts on WhatsApp to more than 20 worker leaders, who passed them on. (Greenpeace India: inside India’s first community-led early warning system for informal workers, https://www.greenpeace.org/india/en/story/18953/beyond-the-forecast-inside-indias-first-community-led-early-warning-system-for-extreme-weather-for-informal-workers/)

- What could stop it: Alerts that tell people to stay indoors when they cannot, and no one listening when they report back.

- Works only if: Each message comes with an action people can take; A named messenger passes it on; Workers can report missing water, shade or help, and someone responds.

Where it has been tried (Reported, not evaluated): Vendors call themselves ‘climate messengers’; workers who cannot read ask them what the board means. (Mongabay India, July 2025, https://india.mongabay.com/2025/07/how-informal-workers-made-weather-warnings-more-effective-this-summer/)

#### Safe water people do not have to buy

Evidence: Reported, not evaluated · Over years

- What to do: Free or cheap drinking water close to where people live and work: piped connections, community water points or refill stations.

- Who it protects: Workers and families who now buy water and drink less than they need when it costs too much.

- Where it suits: Informal settlements and work areas where water has to be bought.

- Who must act: Water authorities, City and local governments, Community and civil society groups

- Running and upkeep: Upkeep of pipes and points, water quality testing, and a fair way to bill or share costs.

- Evidence: In Dhaka, the city water utility worked with local NGOs to bring 3,000 water connections into informal settlements through mini-networks joined to the city system. (Agence Française de Développement: improving access to drinking water in Dhaka’s informal settlements, https://www.afd.fr/en/projects/improve-access-drinking-water-dhakas-informal-settlements)

- What could stop it: Rules that tie a connection to land title, so people in informal settlements cannot get one.

- Works only if: Connections do not require land title; Water is tested and safe; Someone local can fix a broken point fast.

#### Local jobs to install and keep it working

Evidence: Reported, not evaluated · Over years

- What to do: Train and pay local people to install, run and repair cool roofs, water points, shade and green spaces.

- Who it protects: Everyone who depends on the equipment working, and the workers who gain a skill and income.

- Where it suits: Any programme that builds things that need upkeep.

- Who must act: City and local governments, Community and civil society groups, Development banks, donors and climate funds

- Running and upkeep: Wages and training, built into the running budget from the start.

- Evidence: Community-run drinking water plants in Delhi’s low-income settlements created local jobs in running the plants and distributing water. (Kumar, 2024: water security through the Tata Power DDL RO water plants, https://www.researchgate.net/publication/384892155_WATER_SECURITY_THROUGH_CORPORATE_SOCIAL_RESPONSIBILITY_A_CASE_STUDY_OF_RO_WATER_PLANTS_BY_TATA_POWER_DDL)

- What could stop it: Projects that train people once and then stop paying them.

- Works only if: Upkeep jobs are paid for every year; Training leads to real work.

#### Portable shade where there is no wall or tree

Evidence: Design concept · Before the season

- What to do: A light shelter with a bench and shade that can be moved between work sites or fixed to a wall.

- Who it protects: Outdoor workers at sites with no shade at all.

- Where it suits: Short-term sites, roadsides and markets.

- Who must act: Employers and businesses, City and local governments, Community and civil society groups

- Running and upkeep: Moving and fixing it, and repairs; someone must own it.

- Evidence: Bengaluru’s Neralu shelter won a 2024 design contest: about 15 kg, seats four, costs about US$175, and can be carried on an auto-rickshaw. It had not yet been tried by workers when it was shown in May 2025. (AP News, June 2025, via KSAT, https://www.ksat.com/health/2025/06/07/how-an-innovative-portable-shelter-could-help-indias-outdoor-workers-beat-the-heat/)

- What could stop it: Nobody owning it once the pilot ends.

- Works only if: Workers test the design first; Someone owns, moves and repairs it.

Where it has been tried (Reported, not evaluated): In Rewa, Madhya Pradesh, a ₹5,000 grant from the All India Disaster Mitigation Institute let a fruit and vegetable seller buy a large umbrella covering him and his produce, and a way to keep drinking water on his cart, so he no longer had to leave to find water. In Kolkata, a movable plastic sheet gave shade to a utensil seller with no fixed pitch. (AIDMI, southasiadisasters.net Issue 228: Small Heat Resilience Measures, Big Impact in Small Towns and on Small Businesses in India, 2026, https://www.preventionweb.net/publication/documents-and-publications/small-heat-resilience-measures-big-impact-small-towns-and)

#### Paid rest breaks that switch on with the alert

Evidence: Measured in a study · During the heat

- What to do: Agree rest, shade and water breaks that start automatically at each alert level, with earlier or split shifts on the hottest days.

- Who it protects: Construction, farm, delivery, sanitation and street workers.

- Where it suits: Any worksite where an employer, contractor or city department sets the hours.

- Who must act: Employers and businesses, Worker organisations and unions, National governments, City and local governments

- Running and upkeep: Little equipment; the cost is paid time. Someone has to check the rule is kept.

- Evidence: In Singapore, monitors at 24 workplaces found workers could face more heat stress than nearby weather stations reported, so set breaks by heat measured on site. (NUS Project HeatSafe, 2024, https://medicine.nus.edu.sg/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/PRESS-RELEASE_Project-HeatSafe-18MAR2024-FOR-IMMEDIATE-RELEASE.pdf)

- What could stop it: Piece-rate pay and fixed deadlines that make stopping cost money, and no inspection.

- Works only if: Breaks are paid, or paired with income protection; Heat is measured where people work; Shade and water are a few minutes away; Inspectors or unions can check.

Where it has been tried (Measured in a study): Outside Asia, at a sugar producer in Nicaragua, a rest, shade and water programme with La Isla Network raised cane-cutters’ productivity by 19% over five harvests despite shorter days, and cut hospital-treated acute kidney injury by 94%. Pay was changed so workers did not lose money by resting. (Hansson et al., Annals of Work Exposures and Health, 2024, https://doi.org/10.1093/annweh/wxae007)

Where it has been tried (Reported, not evaluated): The same programme was estimated to return about $1.60 for every $1 invested by its third year. (World Economic Forum and BCG, Workforce Heat Resilience: An Actionable Framework to Close the Execution Gap, 2026, https://www.weforum.org/publications/workforce-heat-resilience-an-actionable-framework-to-close-the-execution-gap/)

#### Shade and water on work routes

Evidence: Reported, not evaluated · Before the season

- What to do: Rest shelters with seating, drinking water and rehydration salts along the streets and yards where people work.

- Who it protects: Street vendors, delivery riders, traffic police, sanitation and construction workers.

- Where it suits: Busy junctions, markets and work yards. Misting only in dry, breezy spots.

- Who must act: City and local governments, Employers and businesses, Community and civil society groups

- Running and upkeep: A daily refill and cleaning roster, often ₹500–2,000 a day per water point, and repairs before each season.

- Evidence: Nagpur put shade nets over 10–12 busy junctions in May 2026; several tore or collapsed in strong winds, and residents pointed out the heat had begun at the end of March. (The Hitavada, 11 May 2026, https://www.thehitavada.com//Encyc/2026/5/11/green-nets-at-city-squares-relief-measure-or-another-half-planned-half-planned-civic-experiment.html)

- What could stop it: Nobody named to refill and repair it, or it goes up after the heat has started.

- Works only if: It is in place before the hot season; A named team refills and repairs it; Workers are allowed to stop and use it; Frames are fixed firmly for storms.

#### Income protection when it is too hot to work

Evidence: Measured in a study · Before the season

- What to do: Cash that pays out automatically when heat crosses a set threshold, so workers can afford to stop.

- Who it protects: Informal and daily-wage workers, especially women.

- Where it suits: Where workers belong to an association, cooperative or scheme that can enrol them and pay by phone.

- Who must act: Banks, insurers and financial regulators, Worker organisations and unions, National governments

- Running and upkeep: Premiums or a public subsidy every season, plus enrolment and payment systems.

- Evidence: In a survey of informal workers in Bangkok, nearly 80% had cut their hours because of heat. (WIEGO and HomeNet Thailand, 2025, https://www.wiego.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/WIEGO-Policy-Brief-33-Climate-Change-and-Heat-Stress.pdf)

- What could stop it: A trigger that misses the heat people feel, so they are harmed without a payout, and slow payments.

- Works only if: The trigger counts humidity, not only temperature; Money arrives within days; Workers know they are covered.

Where it has been tried (Reported, not evaluated): In 2026, about 17,000 informal workers in South Asia were covered by parametric heat insurance arranged through People’s Courage International and a local partner, most with premiums paid by companies. Each payout was set at about ₹1,000–3,000, enough for 5–6 days of basic needs, with up to ₹9,000 over a year. These are the programme’s own figures. (World Economic Forum and BCG, Workforce Heat Resilience: An Actionable Framework to Close the Execution Gap, 2026, https://www.weforum.org/publications/workforce-heat-resilience-an-actionable-framework-to-close-the-execution-gap/)

#### Heat-illness first aid on every shift

Evidence: Reported, not evaluated · During the heat

- What to do: Train supervisors and co-workers to spot heat illness, cool a person fast and get help, with water, shade and ice at hand.

- Who it protects: Everyone on the site, especially new and older workers.

- Where it suits: Construction sites, factories, brick kilns and farms with a supervisor.

- Who must act: Employers and businesses, Worker organisations and unions, Health authorities

- Running and upkeep: A refresher before each season, and a steady supply of water and ice.

- Evidence: Doctors at two Indian hospitals with heatstroke units said more than 90% of the patients they treated for heat illness in 2024 were outdoor workers. (Context (Thomson Reuters Foundation), 2024, https://www.context.news/climate-risks/ice-baths-and-ventilators-indias-hospitals-adapt-to-killer-heat)

- What could stop it: Training given once and forgotten, and no transport to a clinic.

- Works only if: Someone trained is on every shift; Everyone knows the emergency number; Treatment is free at the clinic.

Where it has been tried (Reported, not evaluated): Most worker heat illness strikes early: about 80% happens in the first four days on the job. Guidance is to build up new and returning workers’ hours in the heat over 7–14 days, with stricter limits during heatwaves. (World Economic Forum and BCG, Workforce Heat Resilience: An Actionable Framework to Close the Execution Gap, 2026, https://www.weforum.org/publications/workforce-heat-resilience-an-actionable-framework-to-close-the-execution-gap/)

#### Measure and cool hot sheds and factories

Evidence: Measured in a study · Over years

- What to do: Measure heat at the workstations, then cool the roof and walls, add air flow, water and breaks.

- Who it protects: Garment, factory, kiln and warehouse workers, many of them women.

- Where it suits: Indoor workplaces under metal roofs or beside furnaces.

- Who must act: Employers and businesses, Worker organisations and unions, National governments

- Running and upkeep: A heat meter and someone to read it daily; upkeep of roofs and fans; power for ventilation.

- Evidence: At three garment factories in Phnom Penh, workers reporting heat symptoms rose from 68% in the cooler months to 88% in the hot months, by their own reports. (Chea et al., BMC Public Health, 2025, https://bmcpublichealth.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12889-025-22787-0)

- What could stop it: Nobody measuring heat indoors, and factory owners who rent the building.

- Works only if: Heat is measured where people stand; Workers can report symptoms without risk; Fans have power when it is hottest.

Where it has been tried (Reported, not evaluated): Studies summarised for apparel buyers find output falls about 2.6% for each degree of heat stress above 24 °C WBGT. Where toilets are unsafe or missing, women workers often drink less water and suffer worse heat illness, so toilets belong in the plan. (FSG, Managing Heat: From Worker Welfare to Business Resilience, 2026, https://www.fsg.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Managing-Heat-From-Worker-Welfare-to-Business-Resilience_FINAL-4-2-26.pdf)

### Homes

Where people sleep, cook and care for others, often under thin roofs that stay hot after dark.

#### Cool roofs

Evidence: Measured in a study · Before the season

- What to do: A white, solar-reflective coating on tin, asbestos or concrete roofs, so less heat reaches the room below.

- Who it protects: Families in informal and low-income homes, older people, young children and the sick.

- Where it suits: Sound roofs in hot, sunny places, where residents can stay long enough to benefit.

- Who must act: City and local governments, Community and civil society groups, Development banks, donors and climate funds

- Running and upkeep: Recoating every few years, and a thermometer to check it works.

- Evidence: In a two-year trial in Burkina Faso, cool roofs lowered indoor temperatures by 1.2–1.7 °C and residents’ heart rates fell; a trial in about 400 Ahmedabad homes began in 2025. (Reuters, via South China Morning Post, 2025, https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/south-asia/article/3301810/indian-slums-get-cool-roofs-beat-summer-heat)

- What could stop it: Promising degrees nobody measured, renters who cannot change the roof, and no money to recoat.

- Works only if: Rooms are measured before and after; Tenants are protected from rent rises; Someone pays to recoat.

Where it has been tried (Reported, not evaluated): In Dhaka’s Kerail settlement, reflective paint went on 105 buildings, including a day care centre, a school and two garment factories. Indoor air at peak heat fell by 7.72 °C in one building and by 3.5 °C on average; one roof’s surface fell by 12.3 °C. Thin corrugated roofs made it hard to apply, and some local paints were not reflective enough. (Sustainable Energy for All and the Kigali Cooling Efficiency Program, via PreventionWeb, 2021, https://www.preventionweb.net/news/cool-roofs-help-reduce-heatwave-impacts-bangladesh-and-indonesia)

Where it has been tried (Reported, not evaluated): In an industrial building in Indonesia, a 5,200 m² cool roof brought indoor air at noon down from 40.8 °C to 30.4 °C for about 500 shift workers. These are indoor air readings; roof-surface drops are always larger. (Sustainable Energy for All and the Kigali Cooling Efficiency Program, via PreventionWeb, 2021, https://www.preventionweb.net/news/cool-roofs-help-reduce-heatwave-impacts-bangladesh-and-indonesia)

#### Shade the walls and let the air through

Evidence: Measured in a study · Before the season

- What to do: Bamboo blinds, jute screens or awnings on the sunny side, and higher vents that let hot air out at night.

- Who it protects: Everyone indoors, especially at night.

- Where it suits: Most homes; screens are cheap and households can fit them.

- Who must act: Community and civil society groups, City and local governments

- Running and upkeep: Fixing and replacing screens each season; vents need rain and mosquito screens.

- Evidence: In low-income homes measured in Dhaka, Delhi, Faisalabad and rural Maharashtra, tin-roofed houses stayed warmer indoors than outside because they cooled so slowly at night. (Tasgaonkar et al., Scientific Data, 2022, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-022-01314-5)

- What could stop it: Openings that let in dust, rain or intruders, and screens that block all air.

- Works only if: Air can still move; Vents are secure; Someone replaces worn screens.

#### Fans and power people can afford

Evidence: Measured in a study · Over years

- What to do: Efficient fans, lifeline electricity tariffs and reliable supply in the hottest weeks.

- Who it protects: Low-income households without any way to cool down.

- Where it suits: Homes with a grid connection; solar where the grid is weak.

- Who must act: Utilities and energy regulators, City and local governments, National governments

- Running and upkeep: Monthly power bills, and a grid that holds in a heatwave.

- Evidence: 1.12 billion of the rural and urban poor are at high risk because they lack access to cooling. (Sustainable Energy for All, 2023, https://www.seforall.org/our-work/research-analysis/chilling-prospects-series/chilling-prospects-global-access-to-cooling-gaps-2023)

- What could stop it: Power cuts at the hottest hours, and bills people cannot pay.

- Works only if: Power is reliable when it is hottest; Tariffs protect the poorest; Fans are efficient.

#### Cooler, cleaner kitchens

Evidence: Measured in a study · Over years

- What to do: Let heat and smoke out of the kitchen, move cooking to cooler hours, and make cleaner fuel affordable through the season.

- Who it protects: Women and girls who cook, and children near the stove.

- Where it suits: Homes cooking indoors on wood, dung, kerosene or gas.

- Who must act: Community and civil society groups, Utilities and energy regulators, National governments

- Running and upkeep: Fuel costs every month, and upkeep of vents and chimneys.

- Evidence: In Nepal’s Madhesh Province, women cooking in hot, smoky kitchens carry a daily ‘thermal labour’ that falls hardest on women in the poorest single-room homes with little access to clean energy or credit. (Ghimire and others, Frontiers in Public Health, 2025, https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/public-health/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1657267/full)

- What could stop it: Clean fuel bought once but not refilled, and kitchens with no way for air to escape.

- Works only if: Refills stay affordable all season; There is an opening for heat and smoke; Women decide how it is designed.

#### Check on people alone through hot nights

Evidence: Measured in a study · During the heat

- What to do: Neighbours, health workers or volunteers call or visit older, ill and disabled people who live alone, day and night, during alerts.

- Who it protects: Older people, people with disabilities or long-term illness, people living alone.

- Where it suits: Any neighbourhood with a list of who lives alone.

- Who must act: Community and civil society groups, Health authorities, City and local governments

- Running and upkeep: A list kept up to date, and volunteers’ or health workers’ time during alerts.

- Evidence: Data from 47,628 people in 68 countries shows hot nights shorten sleep, with bigger losses for older people and in lower-income countries. (Minor et al., One Earth, 2022, https://orbit.dtu.dk/en/publications/rising-temperatures-erode-human-sleep-globally)

- What could stop it: No list of who lives alone, and calls that stop at sunset.

- Works only if: Someone keeps the list; Calls continue after dark; Callers know when to send help.

### Schools and childcare

Children in hot classrooms learn less and fall ill more easily. Most fixes are small and seasonal.

#### Cool the hottest classrooms first

Evidence: Measured in a study · Before the season

- What to do: A reflective coating or a ventilated second roof over the classrooms that get hottest.

- Who it protects: Pupils and teachers.

- Where it suits: Single-storey schools with metal or concrete roofs.

- Who must act: Schools and education authorities, City and local governments, Development banks, donors and climate funds

- Running and upkeep: A line in the school maintenance budget for recoating; anchors checked before the monsoon.

- Evidence: In the United States, each 1 °F hotter school year without air conditioning cut that year’s learning by about 1%, with the largest losses for disadvantaged students. Effects in Asian classrooms are not yet measured. (Park, Goodman, Hurwitz and Smith, American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, 2020, https://www.aeaweb.org/doi/10.1257/pol.20180612)

- What could stop it: Canopies not anchored for monsoon winds, and no budget to recoat.

- Works only if: Classroom heat is logged before and after; There is money to maintain it.

#### Water, and time to drink it

Evidence: Official guidance or data · Before the season

- What to do: Enough safe, cool drinking water for every child, with breaks in the timetable to use it.

- Who it protects: Every pupil, especially the youngest.

- Where it suits: Every school.

- Who must act: Schools and education authorities, Water authorities

- Running and upkeep: Filter changes, cleaning and a supply that lasts the hottest weeks.

- Evidence: Heatwaves disrupted schooling for an estimated 171 million students in 2024, and South Asia was the most affected region. (UNICEF, 2025, https://www.unicef.org/reports/learning-interrupted-global-snapshot-2024)

- What could stop it: One tap for hundreds of children, or filters nobody changes.

- Works only if: Enough taps for the number of children; Teachers build drinking into the day.

#### Heat-ready timetables

Evidence: Reported, not evaluated · During the heat

- What to do: Start earlier, shorten the hottest afternoons, move exams and sports, and keep learning going if schools must close.

- Who it protects: Pupils, teachers and parents who travel in the heat.

- Where it suits: Education departments and school boards, set before the season.

- Who must act: Schools and education authorities, National governments, Weather and climate services

- Running and upkeep: Little money; it needs agreed triggers and a plan for remote or make-up learning.

- Evidence: Bangladesh closed schools for about 33 million children in its April 2024 heatwave, and Cambodia cut the school day by two hours. (NBC News, 2024, https://www.nbcnews.com/news/world/schools-close-extreme-heat-philippines-bangladesh-asia-rcna149485)

- What could stop it: Closing schools with no plan for learning, and decisions made on the day.

- Works only if: Triggers are agreed before the season; There is a plan to make up lost learning.

#### Shaded play space

Evidence: Measured in a study · Over years

- What to do: Trees, shade structures and less hard paving where children play and queue.

- Who it protects: Children at break times and assembly.

- Where it suits: Schools with open yards and a water source.

- Who must act: Schools and education authorities, City and local governments, Community and civil society groups

- Running and upkeep: Watering through the holidays, when nobody is at school.

- Evidence: Researchers studying how age groups use green spaces found children wanted trees for shade and places to play: ask them before you design. (Frantzeskaki et al., chapter 11 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023, https://doi.org/10.4337/9781800376762)

- What could stop it: Planting that dies in the first summer break.

- Works only if: Someone waters through the holidays; Children help choose where shade goes.

### Health facilities

Clinics and hospitals fill up in a heatwave just as power, water and staff come under strain.

#### Ready to cool heatstroke patients fast

Evidence: Official guidance or data · During the heat

- What to do: Rapid assessment and active cooling of suspected heatstroke, with ice packs, IV fluids, rehydration salts and trained staff.

- Who it protects: Anyone with heat illness, above all outdoor workers and older people.

- Where it suits: Every hospital and health centre in heat-prone districts.

- Who must act: Health authorities, National governments

- Running and upkeep: Stocks of ice, fluids and medicines through the season, and training every year.

- Evidence: In June 2024 India’s health ministry asked central government hospitals to set up special heatwave units, and advised rapid assessment and active cooling of suspected heatstroke, with stocks of rehydration salts, IV fluids and ice packs. (Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, India, press release, 19 June 2024, https://mohfw.gov.in/press-info/7538)

- What could stop it: Supplies that run out at the peak, and staff who have never practised the protocol.

- Works only if: Staff train before the season; Ice and fluids are stocked early; Care for heat illness is free.

#### Keep the power on and the building cool

Evidence: Official guidance or data · Over years

- What to do: Backup or solar power, cooling in waiting and treatment areas, and cool roofs, shading and rainwater harvesting.

- Who it protects: Patients, staff, and medicines and vaccines that spoil in heat.

- Where it suits: Facilities on weak grids or under hot roofs, especially in rural areas.

- Who must act: Health authorities, Utilities and energy regulators, Development banks, donors and climate funds

- Running and upkeep: Fuel or battery upkeep, servicing of cooling, and a power company that prioritises the facility.

- Evidence: About 12% of health facilities in low- and lower-middle-income countries in South Asia have no electricity at all, and rural facilities are worse served than urban ones. (WHO fact sheet: electricity in health-care facilities, 2023, https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/electricity-in-health-care-facilities)

- What could stop it: Backup generators with no fuel budget, and cooling nobody services.

- Works only if: The power company knows the facility comes first; Someone services the backup; There is a running budget.

#### Protect the staff

Evidence: Measured in a study · During the heat

- What to do: Cool rest rooms, drinking water, and shorter rotations for staff in full protective gear.

- Who it protects: Nurses, doctors, community health workers and cleaners.

- Where it suits: Wards, emergency rooms and outreach teams in hot weather.

- Who must act: Health authorities, Worker organisations and unions

- Running and upkeep: Staff time for rotations, and a cooled rest space.

- Evidence: Across 3,082 health workers in India, Indonesia, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam, poor practices with protective equipment were linked to heat-related symptoms. (Yang et al., BMC Nursing, 2024, https://doi.org/10.1186/s12912-024-01770-x)

- What could stop it: Too few staff to rotate during a surge.

- Works only if: Rotas plan for the surge; Staff can report symptoms early.

#### A surge plan linked to the warning

Evidence: Independently evaluated · During the heat

- What to do: Extra beds, staff and supplies that switch on with each alert level, agreed with the weather service and the city.

- Who it protects: Everyone who falls ill in a heatwave.

- Where it suits: District and city health systems with a heat warning.

- Who must act: Health authorities, Weather and climate services, City and local governments

- Running and upkeep: Planning time before the season, and overtime or reserve staff during alerts.

- Evidence: After Ahmedabad’s heat action plan prepared hospitals and warned the public, an estimated 1,190 deaths a year were avoided. (Hess et al., Journal of Environmental and Public Health, 2018, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6236972/)

- What could stop it: Warnings that reach the public but not the hospital.

- Works only if: Hospitals receive the alert directly; Each level names what the hospital does.

#### Shade and water for people waiting outside

Evidence: Official guidance or data · Before the season

- What to do: Shade, seating and drinking water where patients queue, and appointment slots so fewer wait at midday.

- Who it protects: Patients and carers, especially older people, pregnant women and children.

- Where it suits: Outpatient departments, health centres and vaccination days.

- Who must act: Health authorities, City and local governments

- Running and upkeep: Someone to refill water and keep the space usable.

- Evidence: India’s June 2024 advisory asked facilities in heat-prone areas to provide shade outside, and cooling in waiting areas. (Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, India, press release, 19 June 2024, https://mohfw.gov.in/press-info/7538)

- What could stop it: Shade built where the queue isn’t.

- Works only if: It is where people actually wait; Someone refills the water.

### Markets and neighbourhoods

The streets, markets, stops and public spaces where people spend the hottest hours.

#### Shade and water in markets, designed with vendors

Evidence: Measured in a study · Before the season

- What to do: Shade over stalls and aisles, and drinking water points, planned and run with the vendors’ association.

- Who it protects: Street vendors and their customers.

- Where it suits: Open and street markets.

- Who must act: City and local governments, Community and civil society groups, Worker organisations and unions

- Running and upkeep: Storm-proof fixing, replacing worn cloth, and a refill and cleaning roster.

- Evidence: Of 721 Delhi street vendors surveyed in April and May 2024, 80% saw fewer customers during heatwaves and 49% lost income. (Greenpeace India and National Hawkers Federation, 2024, https://www.greenpeace.org/india/en/press/16737/new-report-by-greenpeace-india-and-national-hawkers-federation-reveals-harsh-heatwave-toll-on-street-vendors/)

- What could stop it: Beautification that pushes informal vendors out, and shade that blocks fire access.

- Works only if: Vendors have a say in design and upkeep; Nobody is evicted to make room.

Where it has been tried (Reported, not evaluated): Young women vendors in Ahmedabad, who already sell 8 to 12 and 4 to 8 to avoid the midday heat, asked for shared shade sails covering about ten sellers each, and a licensed, fixed place to sell. (AIDMI, southasiadisasters.net Issue 228: Small Heat Resilience Measures, Big Impact in Small Towns and on Small Businesses in India, 2026, https://www.preventionweb.net/publication/documents-and-publications/small-heat-resilience-measures-big-impact-small-towns-and)

#### Cool waiting points

Evidence: Measured in a study · Before the season

- What to do: Shade, a bench, drinking water and the heat alert on a board, at bus stops, ration shops and other queues.

- Who it protects: Commuters, older and disabled people, carers with children.

- Where it suits: Busy stops and queues with no shade.

- Who must act: City and local governments, Community and civil society groups

- Running and upkeep: Refilling the water, and keeping access clear for wheelchairs.

- Evidence: Measuring how hot people feel on summer days, researchers found shade from buildings cooled most by day, then trees, then light structures such as sails. (Middel et al., 50 Grades of Shade, Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society, https://par.nsf.gov/biblio/10230332-grades-shade)

- What could stop it: Counting shelters built instead of people protected.

- Works only if: It is where people actually wait; Older and disabled people can reach it.

#### Cooling centres people can actually use

Evidence: Official guidance or data · During the heat

- What to do: Cool public spaces, such as libraries, community halls or places of worship, opened during alerts, with water and somewhere to sit.

- Who it protects: People with no cool place at home, and outdoor workers on breaks.

- Where it suits: Neighbourhoods with many hot homes and a suitable public building nearby.

- Who must act: City and local governments, Community and civil society groups, Health authorities

- Running and upkeep: Staff, power and water for every alert day, and transport for those who cannot walk there.

- Evidence: A review of the evidence and strategies for running cooling centres to prevent heat-related illness. (US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, in the GHHIN resource library, https://heathealth.info/wp-content/uploads/cdc_47657_DS1-compressed-1.pdf)

- What could stop it: A cooled building nobody can reach, open at the wrong hours, or a worker who cannot leave work to use it.

- Works only if: People can reach it, including those who can’t walk far; It opens at the right hours, evenings too; Power and water are secure; Someone staffs and funds it; Workers are free to leave work to use it.

#### Trees that survive

Evidence: Measured in a study · Over years

- What to do: Look after existing trees first; plant heat-hardy species where people walk and wait, with water and three years of care.

- Who it protects: Pedestrians, vendors and everyone waiting outside.

- Where it suits: Streets and open spaces with root space and a water source.

- Who must act: City and local governments, Water authorities, Community and civil society groups

- Running and upkeep: Watering and care for at least three years after planting.

- Evidence: In one Berlin park more than 500 of 870 new trees died within ten years despite watering: count trees that survive, not saplings planted. (Hansen et al., chapter 10 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023, https://doi.org/10.4337/9781800376762)

- What could stop it: No water plan, and counting saplings instead of canopy.
